articles.title_orig: China continues suspending part of control measures on dual-use items export to US
articles.title_zh: China continues suspending part of control measures on dual-use items export to US
articles.content_orig:
BEIJING – China will extend the suspension of part of its export control measures on dual-use items to the United States from Nov 28, 2026, to Jan 27, 2027, the Ministry of Commerce said Tuesday.
The suspension of the second clause of the Announcement No 46 of 2024 was first announced in November 2025 and was originally scheduled to run through Nov 27, 2026.
According to the clause, now suspended, the export of dual-use items related to gallium, germanium, antimony and superhard materials to the United States is not to be permitted in principle, while stricter examinations on end-users and end-use purposes are to be conducted regarding exports of the dual-use item of graphite to the United States.

articles.content_orig:
Pakistani astronaut launches into space aboard Chinese rocket

articles.title_orig: China launches Shenzhou-24 crew, setting up a year-long orbital stay for one astronaut
articles.title_zh: China launches Shenzhou-24 crew, setting up a year-long orbital stay for one astronaut
articles.content_orig:
China on Wednesday launched the Shenzhou 24 spacecraft with three astronauts — two Chinese and a Pakistani — sending the first foreign crew member to its space station .
Pakistani astronaut Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, 40, is flying alongside Chinese astronauts Tang Hongbo, 51, and Wu Yi, 39, after the craft blasted off from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwestern China on Wednesday morning. It successfully separated from a rocket and entered its predetermined orbit.
The launch marked the first joint flight involving Chinese and foreign astronauts in the history of China's manned space program.
Hours earlier, crowds of people attended a send-off ceremony, with many holding up their phones to capture the moment.
The crew will conduct more than 90 scientific experiments and technology tests during their mission, official Chinese news agency Xinhua earlier reported. Ali will conduct a photosynthetic cyanobacteria experiment in orbit during his short-term mission before returning to Earth aboard the Shenzhou 23 spacecraft, it said.
Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif offered his best wishes to the astronauts ahead of their mission.
"Pakistan-China friendship is surpassing the heights of the Himalayas in its journey to outer space," he said on X on Tuesday.
The joint flight is part of an agreement signed by China and Pakistan in February 2025.
While this was the first spaceflight for Ali and Wu, Tang has flown on two previous missions and is set to become the first astronaut to board the Tiangong space station three times, national broadcaster CCTV said.
At a news conference on Tuesday, Tang said that differences in language, culture and psychology had made learning to work together more challenging on this mission, but that both sides' efforts were paying off.
In front of reporters, those efforts were reflected in Ali's Mandarin proficiency. He cited a line of Chinese poetry about climbing one story higher to see farther.
"It's like my daily training. Day after day, reaching new heights," he said in Mandarin.
Speaking in English, he said he hoped the next chapter of space cooperation between the two countries would go from one astronaut in one flight to multiple joint flights and to the moon, Mars and beyond.
In May, China launched Shenzhou 23 , which carried three astronauts, including one crew member who was set to remain in space for about a year.
China is preparing for its first crewed lunar landing by 2030. The U.S. is widely seen as China's main space rival, with NASA aiming to land astronauts on the lunar surface in 2028.

articles.title_orig: Trump Weighs Fresh Tariffs on India and China: What is Behind the US Trade Investigation?
articles.title_zh: Trump Weighs Fresh Tariffs on India and China: What is Behind the US Trade Investigation?
articles.content_orig:
For a minute there, it seemed like someone in the Trump administration might actually be willing to stand up to China.
For about a week and a half, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent was the face of an emerging harder line on Nvidia over the potential risks its co-founder Jensen Huang 's affairs posed to national security. Bessent was giving voice to China hawks who had felt sidelined by the Trump administration's willingness to sell artificial intelligence chips to  China.
They see China's AI program as a major threat, and want to restrain its growth by cutting off the supply of advanced chips to China. The resignation of Huang, who pressed the Trump Administration to allow the exports, seemed to signal that the hawks had found new influence in Washington.
By this weekend, Bessent had softened his public resistance to Huang's reinstatement. That came just in time for Nvidia's board to reappoint Huang as CEO at President Donald Trump 's urging.
Whether any real damage was done to national security isn't clear. But it is safe to say that the incoming Democratic majority in Congress won't take Trump at his word when he said on CNBC Monday that the Department of Justice "did a pretty good investigation" that exonerated Huang.
Congress will look deeply into the worries Bessent himself raised about Huang's acknowledged romantic relationship with a woman The New York Times and others have reported was a Chinese intelligence asset.
Nvidia's board said it had received assurances from top U.S. officials and had concluded his return wasn't a national security risk.
A top concern is whether China was able to use the affair to help divert Nvidia's high-end artificial intelligence chips toward helping its military. Bessent in a Nov. 13 interview with CNBC outlined the stakes.
"Any leakage is very frustrating because it hurts the — it hurts our great companies and in the AI race it gives the Chinese an advantage," he said.
Bessent said that his department and others had wanted to blacklist Megaspeed, the company previously run by Alice Huang, Jensen Huang's paramour. But "Commerce has the pen," Bessent said.
The Commerce Department is headed by Secretary Howard Lutnick, Bessent's rival.
Putting Huang back at Nvidia wasn't originally Bessent's preference. He said in a Fox interview on Nov. 15 that the board should "go outside the company" to find a new leader. But by this past weekend, Bessent had apparently gotten on board with Trump's wishes.
"Jensen is on the outside now," Bessent told CBS on Sunday, in trying to explain his apparent policy shift.
Commerce has since taken steps to tighten some restrictions meant to prevent U.S. chips from helping China advance in the AI race.
But there is bipartisan worry about the Nvidia episode. "I think we need to catalog the damage that's been done," Sen. Tom Cotton, R-Ark., told The Wall Street Journal . He said Lutnick had not responded to letters he sent saying the administration should be "taking the threats of communist China more seriously."
But Trump has clearly put an upper limit on how aggressively anyone in his administration can push back on China. The president said Monday that he was swayed by the pageantry in his visit to China last week.
Xi "met me at the plane, which is something they've never done, which was a sign," Trump said.
Trump said he felt like he needed to intervene to back Huang because the stock market was plummeting in the wake of Nvidia's troubles — a development he also blamed on Democrats' midterm victory.
"I watched our country lose $5 trillion because of a bad election," he said. "If I didn't get involved, you'd probably have a very sad Nvidia for a long time to come." Now, its stock performance will be "unbelievable."
Bessent on Sunday played down the market risks. The company "continues to be fantastically profitable, and there is near unlimited demand for their chips worldwide," he told CBS.
Lutnick has embraced Trump's transactional urges. He has backed deals in which the U.S. takes equity stakes in companies such as Intel, saying the taxpayer deserves some of the upside.
Lutnick in January said he had heard Huang pitch Trump on allowing Nvidia to sell its relatively more advanced H200 chips into China.
"There are strong — two sides. We shouldn't sell them any or we should sell them." Where does he stand? "Right in the middle," Lutnick told Bloomberg . Trump decided to go ahead with the deal.
Bessent has said he is "neither a hawk nor a dove" on China, and is simply trying to manage the ultra-sensitive relationship between the world's two biggest economies. But the upshot of the Huang affair seems to be that Bessent wasn't able to sway the president on a matter that seemed cut-and-dried just days ago.
Lutnick, meanwhile, is riding high.
Trump said he discussed whether Huang should return to Nvidia with Lutnick, Bessent and Vice President JD Vance. "Howard Lutnick was very good. Very, he's very professional," Trump said on CNBC Monday.
"I call them the opposites, Scott and Howard," Trump added, before declaring them "both good."

articles.title_orig: China's Huawei says US conviction 'without legal or factual merit'
articles.title_zh: China's Huawei says US conviction 'without legal or factual merit'
articles.content_orig:
A United States jury has convicted Chinese tech giant Huawei Technologies of conspiracy to steal trade secrets and bank fraud as it grew into one of the world’s biggest suppliers of gear for wireless telecommunications networks.
However, jurors on Tuesday acquitted the company of the most serious charge it faced: engaging in a criminal racketeering conspiracy. The charge is typically used in organised crime and drug cases, but prosecutors used it to accuse Huawei of operating in an illicit fashion to steal intellectual property from US companies.
The verdict followed a lengthy trial in which US prosecutors argued that Huawei repeatedly stole technological secrets from competitors and partners in the US and elsewhere.
Huawei was also accused of doing business in countries subject to US sanctions, including Iran and North Korea, and making false statements to US government officials and banks as part of an effort to hide its misdeeds.
US authorities had targeted Huawei for years, saying the company posed national security risks.
The criminal case began in 2018, and the following year the US government placed Huawei on a trade blacklist that restricted its access to US technology.
Experts have said the case has not undermined Huawei’s business, as the company diversified and emerged as a key player in China’s push for artificial intelligence.
The trial lasted more than two months, with prosecutors calling more than 60 witnesses and the defence calling 15.
Huawei and three affiliates faced 12 charges, including racketeering conspiracy, bank fraud, wire fraud, sanctions violations, and conspiring to steal trade secrets and obstruct justice.
Lawyers for the company said US investigators had used isolated episodes of wrongdoing by a few of Huawei’s more than 200,000 employees to spin a false narrative about a grand conspiracy that did not actually exist.
Huawei lawyer Brian Heberlig said the company would appeal the convictions but saw the racketeering conspiracy acquittal as vindication.
“That was the only count that brought all of the allegations together,” and the jury rejected it, he said outside court, saying that the verdict “repudiated the central government narrative in the case”.
It is unclear what effect the verdict might have on Huawei’s global fortunes. The company hasn’t been allowed to sell equipment to US carriers for years because of security concerns. It has also been blacklisted by other Western allies, including Canada and the United Kingdom.
The case emerged in December 2018 when Meng Wanzhou, Huawei’s chief financial officer and daughter of the company’s founder, was detained in Canada on a US warrant, prompting a diplomatic crisis involving the US, China and Canada.
Meng had been secretly indicted for allegedly misleading an HSBC banker about Huawei’s business in Iran, so the company could move dollars in and out of Iran in violation of US sanctions.
She fought extradition to the US for nearly three years, before entering a deferred prosecution agreement and flying home to China to a hero’s welcome. The charges against her were dropped.
The 2018 indictment alleged that Huawei misled HSBC, Standard Chartered and BNP Paribas about its business dealings in Iran.
Prosecutors added new charges in 2020, including that Huawei conspired to steal trade secrets from US technology companies over two decades.
During the trial, prosecutors tried to prove Huawei stole source code from Cisco Systems for its routers, stole wireless telecommunications company Quintel’s antenna technology, and hired a professor to gain access to a circuit board developed by semiconductor company CNEX.
Jurors watched a video that, according to prosecutors, showed a Huawei employee slipping a piece of a T-Mobile testing robot into his backpack, and heard about a Huawei engineer sneaking into a Fujitsu booth at a trade show to photograph a device.
Prosecutors gave jurors a statement attached to Meng’s deferred prosecution agreement, in which she acknowledged that the company illegally conducted business in Iran. She did not testify at trial, though an HSBC banker she met with in 2013 did testify.
The defence argued that HSBC and the other banks knew about Huawei’s business in Iran and were competing for Huawei’s business.
Heberlig accused prosecutors during his closing argument of having “cherry-picked” a handful of disparate incidents to support their claim of a 20-year conspiracy.
He said Huawei succeeded through “hard work, innovation, and investment in research and development”.
Huawei has more than 200,000 employees and operates in approximately 170 countries.

articles.title_orig: U.S.-China tensions could rise in 2027, but China could keep growing its exports: Economist
articles.title_zh: U.S.-China tensions could rise in 2027, but China could keep growing its exports: Economist
articles.content_orig:
China is "actively working to suppress India's rise," even as the relationship between the two major Asian powers has thawed in the past year, according to a U.S. panel that sees an opening for greater outreach to India.
On Nov. 18, a U.S. China Economic and Security Review Commission report said Beijing is applying military, economic, maritime, and other forms of pressure to constrain India .
China has recalled engineers and withheld equipment to slow India's electronics manufacturing, slashed pharmaceutical input prices to undercut new Indian plants, and imposed export controls on battery technology to impede the development of India's clean energy industry, the report said.
It added that these tensions offer the U.S. an opportunity to counter growing Chinese influence by building closer ties with India across key sectors such as pharmaceutical and defense.
Ties have improved since a deadly border skirmish in 2020, but experts told CNBC that trust is still thin between Beijing and New Delhi. However, they added that the uneasy peace with China is unlikely to make India align automatically with the U.S. as an ally.
The Indian foreign and commerce ministries and the Chinese foreign ministry did not respond to emails seeking comments.
The thawing in relations between India and China came amid industrial demand, as well as the need for "a whole lot of posturing for the U.S.," said Arpit Chaturvedi, South Asia advisor at strategic advisory firm Teneo.
Over the past year, India faced tariff pressures and needed to signal to Washington that its options remain open, including that of renegotiating relations with China, he explained, but added that as the trade deal with the U.S. is "close enough now," there is no pressing need for that signaling.
Further improvement in the relationship is also limited by reports of renewed border tensions between the two sides and Beijing's scant reciprocation on easing access to technology and people movement, he said.
Last month, an Indian military official said that confrontations with Chinese soldiers were ongoing across several locations along the country's northeastern border, even as top leaders from the countries met with fanfare at the BRICS Summit in September.
Another flash point was when Beijing put export controls on tunnel boring machines last month. "Our relations with China remain good, and if there aren't any new hurdles , they can improve further," India's Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal reportedly said after China's move to tighten TBM exports.
On Monday, a Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson reportedly said Beijing is ready to work with India to facilitate visa arrangements for business personnel from both sides amid reports that fewer Indian businessmen got visas to attend an annual trade fair in Shanghai.
The Chinese "actively disrupt" areas where India is trying to make progress in terms of moving global supply chains, developing advanced industrial technologies such as EVs, batteries, electronic components, and pharmaceutical ingredients, Pramit Pal Chaudhuri, South Asia practice head at Eurasia Group, told CNBC.
He added China is increasingly focused on containing India economically rather than through military overtures.
India's manufacturing push still relies on Chinese inputs, from electronics components and solar materials to rare earth magnets and specialized machinery. Between April and October, India imported goods worth $96.6 billion from China , up more than 30% from a year ago, as per commerce ministry data released earlier this month.
Its major imports from China include electronic goods, machinery, chemicals, transport equipment, iron and steel, and pharmaceutical products.
While India needs inputs for its manufacturing ambitions from Beijing and China values access to Indian markets, trust between the two sides is "still thin," according to Reema Bhattacharya, head of Asia research at risk intelligence company Verisk Maplecroft, citing a large trade imbalance and overlapping interests in South Asia and the Indian Ocean as additional issues.

articles.title_orig: Trump says pardon is always an option for Jensen Huang, and that pleading the Fifth isn’t necessary
articles.title_zh: Trump says pardon is always an option for Jensen Huang, and that pleading the Fifth isn’t necessary
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump said that while pardoning Jensen Huang for any potential criminal activity remains an option, he doesn’t think that will be needed for the newly reinstated Nvidia CEO .
“It’s always an option, I guess, but I don’t think it’ll be necessary,” Trump told the New York Post in an interview published Tuesday night.
Asked about Huang’s scheduled appearances next week on Capitol Hill, Trump said, “I don’t think he needs to take the Fifth. I think it’s an interesting story for people.”
“I think I want him to just tell the truth, and I mean, his lawyers are going to have to advise him, but I’ve always found him to be 100% aboveboard, and you know a very smart person,” the president said.
A representative for Huang declined to comment on Trump’s comments. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for further comment.
Speaking at a news conference Tuesday, Attorney General Todd Blanche indicated he would have told Trump if Huang had been involved in any criminal activity.
“To the extent that, that the department, that the Department of Justice had information that he was committing crimes or something like this, that is, that is, that’s just not, that’s something that I would have certainly told the president had it been true,” Blanche said.
In Congress, lawmakers on both sides of the aisle are preparing to grill Huang over their national security concerns.
A spokesperson for the Republican-led House Intelligence Committee told NBC News that Huang’s reinstatement “changes nothing” and that there “are serious questions on national security implications that still need answers.”
Huang and Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter are expected to sit for transcribed interviews next Tuesday and Wednesday before the House Select Committee on China, the House Intelligence Committee and the House Foreign Affairs Committee.
Huang, who has not been charged with a crime, resigned from his post as CEO of the chip giant following reports that he had a relationship with a woman who U.S. intelligence agencies believed was a Chinese spy. In a Nov. 8 memo to Nvidia’s staff, he said, “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”
Trump worked behind the scenes over the weekend to get Nvidia’s board to bring Huang back. That move has been met with bipartisan backlash.
Sen. Pete Ricketts, R-Neb., on Monday raised concerns over Nvidia’s quick reversal to rehire Huang after indicating it wouldn’t.
“His own board described his behavior as lacking ‘candor.’ I’ve served on a public company board. His behavior does not support reinstatement,” Ricketts wrote in a post on X.
Sen. Kevin Cramer, R-N.D., wrote that with Nvidia’s rehiring of Huang, “the national security risk is passed along to the United States military and its citizens.”
Cramer and Ricketts are both members of the Senate Banking Committee, where Huang is scheduled to testify in public Dec. 3.
In celebrating Huang’s return, Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social post that the U.S. government “has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security.”
Similarly, Nvidia’s board said it reached the decision to reinstate Huang after receiving “input from senior levels of the United States government” that his “reinstatement poses no national security risk.”
Kyla Guilfoil is a breaking news reporter on the politics team for NBC News Digital.

articles.title_orig: Trump open to pardoning Jensen Huang if needed: NY Post
articles.title_zh: Trump open to pardoning Jensen Huang if needed: NY Post
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump said he would be willing to pardon reinstated Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang if needed after Huang appears before Congress next week, according to an exclusive interview with the New York Post.
Huang's reinstatement followed Trump's intervention with Nvidia's board, including a reported call into a board meeting to argue for his return. Even so, lawmakers are still set to scrutinize his relationship with suspected Chinese intelligence asset Alice Huang in two appearances next week.
Nvidia shares surged 31% on Monday after Huang was reinstated as CEO, before falling 5.9% on Tuesday amid a broader market pullback.
Trump also said that Huang should not need to invoke the Fifth Amendment to avoid self-incrimination when he appears for a closed-door interview with the House Foreign Affairs Committee on Dec. 1 and before the Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 3.
"I think it's an interesting story for people," Trump said, according to the NY Post. "I think I want him to just tell the truth."
Trump added that while a pardon was "always an option," he did not think it would be "necessary," the newspaper reported. The president's clemency authority is limited to federal offenses, according to the Justice Department's Office of the Pardon Attorney.
Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., told Fox News on Monday that he expected Huang to invoke his Fifth Amendment rights during the congressional proceedings.
"I expect him to take the Fifth Amendment so he doesn't incriminate himself in criminal prosecution, but we're going to give him a chance to explain," Kennedy said.
Trump also told the New York Post that he was open to the U.S. government taking an equity stake in Nvidia, similar to its stake in Intel in 2025, arguing that the company's success was vital to maintaining the U.S. lead in artificial intelligence.
He also said it was his understanding that Huang had not had affairs with other women linked to Beijing and that he did not know how many affairs Huang had acknowledged.
Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md., the lead Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee, told CNBC on Tuesday that he believed Trump was making decisions that could benefit his own stock portfolio, despite the president's assertion that he does not make trades himself.
"If you don't believe that, you're too innocent to be let out of the house by yourself. The whole thing is a money-making operation. What's the alternative explanation?" Raskin said.
Separately, independent journalist Marisa Kabas reported that Huang told Nvidia employees at Tuesday's all-hands meeting that Trump "loves" the company because of its employees' "contributions" to the U.S., while also addressing questions about whether Nvidia had become political or partisan.
"I want to be very clear: President Trump is the United States president. I'll do everything I can to help this president be informed about how he can make decisions in the best interests of the country," Huang said.
The reinstated CEO added that it would be a "great honor and a privilege" to go to Washington, D.C., to "inform them so the government can make the best possible decision," and said he would do the same for whoever becomes the next president.
"Don't think for a second politics played a role in the company. We are the most apolitical company. Everything he's done is because of his affection, admiration, and recognition of the great company that you are," Huang said.

articles.title_orig: Watch out, AlphaFold: Claude and ChatGPT’s new biology skills wow scientists
articles.title_zh: Watch out, AlphaFold: Claude and ChatGPT’s new biology skills wow scientists
articles.content_orig:
Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain
            the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in
            Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles
            and JavaScript.
Accurately predicting protein structures has been the preserve of specialist AI tools like AlphaFold — but now general-purpose models are catching up. Credit: EMBL-EBI (CC0)
Earlier this month, Xinming Tu set out to test what artificial-intelligence models know about proteins. Tu, a researcher at an AI biology company called Phylo in South San Francisco, California, asked large language models (LLMs) from OpenAI, Anthropic and Google to predict the sequences of obscure bacterial proteins.
He left the analysis to run overnight and woke up shocked at the results. The latest versions of Anthropic’s Claude models had outperformed other LLMs — but also specialized ‘protein language models’, which are trained on vast troves of sequence data and specially designed for such tasks.
Scientists are using AI to dream up revolutionary new proteins
Scientists are using AI to dream up revolutionary new proteins
When Tu and Leo Chen, a computational biologist at Harvard Medical School in Boston, Massachusetts, shared the results in a 16 November blogpost , it set off a frenzy among computational biologists to see what other protein biology LLMs such as Claude could do. For instance, Tu and Chen and others have found it could perform a key step in protein-structure prediction.
And on 24 November, OpenAI announced that its latest language models had successfully designed new proteins, some of which behaved as expected when made and tested in the lab. The results hint that the latest LLMs might be gaining a sophisticated understanding of protein biology.
The research has kicked off a debate over the future of biological AI . Some scientists predict that ‘general purpose’ models such as Claude and ChatGPT will eventually outperform specialist tools such as AlphaFold at tasks including protein structure prediction and design.
“We want to see a world where a scientist can just describe in natural language what they want a ChatGPT model to do, and the model can just be infinitely flexible and design exactly what the person wants,” says Joy Jiao, who leads life-sciences research at OpenAI in San Francisco, California.
But some researchers question the extent to which LLMs are learning underlying lessons in protein biology. They suggest that some of their abilities could be the result of regurgitating training data.
The release of AlphaFold2, Google DeepMind’s blockbuster protein-structure-prediction AI , in 2020 launched a revolution in biological AI. There is now a vast ecosystem of software — much of it open source — for modelling different properties of proteins, such as how they interact with possible drugs, and for designing new proteins.
Researchers have begun using LLMs to orchestrate these specialist models, but it has mostly been as a time-saving measure, says Martin Pačesa, a structural biologist at the University of Zurich. “In most cases, a specialist will always perform better than a generalist for a given task,” he says.
Five protein-design questions that still challenge AI
Five protein-design questions that still challenge AI
To see if an LLM could stand in for specialist protein-design tools, Jiao and her colleagues asked an OpenAI model called GPT-6.2 to design 3D protein structures capable of binding to five different biological targets, including proteins implicated in cancer and immune disorders. After the LLMs generated the designs, the researchers used a specialist AI tool to determine a corresponding genetic sequence. Lab experiments confirmed that around 11% of designs were able to bind their target.
In other experiments, the OpenAI team showed that its LLMs could design protein sequences, redesign existing antibodies, and other tasks typically performed by specialist tools. In some cases, the LLM performed as well as some specialist tools, and in others, such as predicting the 3D structure of proteins, it was far off. OpenAI researchers describe the work in a blogpost and technical paper .
Jiao emphasizes that the work is a proof of principle, and that specialized AI tools were still needed for key steps. But Masatoshi Uehara, an OpenAI researcher who was part of the effort, believes that LLMs will only get better at protein biology. “I believe the large language model can technically beat every specialized model in even each capability,” he says.

articles.title_orig: Stocks retreat as AI rebound stumbles, tariff threats loom
articles.title_zh: Stocks retreat as AI rebound stumbles, tariff threats loom
articles.content_orig:
Asian stock markets have fallen sharply as doubts continue to swirl over the AI boom, reversing a rally sparked by Jensen Huang’s return as CEO of Nvidia.
Taiwan’s stock market led the sell-off, with the benchmark Taiex plunging as much as 7.9 percent in morning trading.
South Korea’s Kospi fell more than 6 percent, while Japan’s Nikkei 225 dropped 3.6 percent.
Tech stocks linked to the AI trade suffered some of the steepest losses.
In Japan, Tokyo Electron, a leading manufacturer of semiconductor fabrication equipment, dived 13.5 percent, while Advantest, a producer of chip testing equipment, plunged 14.5 percent.
South Korea’s Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, the top two memory chip makers globally, sank 9.1 percent and 9.9 percent, respectively.
In Taiwan, TSMC, the world’s biggest contract chip maker, and Apple supplier Foxconn both dropped more than 9 percent.
Hong Kong’s Hang Seng Index bucked the trend, rising as much as 1.3 percent.
The retreat comes after Asian markets surged on Tuesday following Huang’s surprise reinstatement at the helm of chip giant Nvidia following the intervention US President Donald Trump.
Nvidia’s reappointment of Huang, who resigned amid claims he was romantically involved with a woman suspected of working with Chinese intelligence, on Monday sent the chip giant’s New York-listed shares up 31.5 percent, the largest single-day gain US stock market history.
Wall Street saw modest losses on Tuesday after a buying spree during the previous session, with the S&P 500 falling 0.5 percent and the Nasdaq composite down 1.5 percent.
Markets have experienced wild swings over the past month amid the Nvidia scandal and expectations Democrats will push for greater regulation of AI following their sweeping victories in the US midterm elections.
Those headwinds have added to existing concerns that tech firms may not be able to sustain their multi-trillion-dollar investments underpinning the AI boom.
Big Tech’s debt-fuelled splurge has stirred intense debate about whether it is investing in a gold mine in the making or a massive stock market bubble.
Global AI-related investment is forecast to reach $2.7 trillion this year and $3.6 trillion in 2027, according to technology insights company Gartner.

articles.title_orig: Yemen’s Houthis Take Second Swipe at Tallest Tower in Saudi Capital
articles.title_zh: Yemen’s Houthis Take Second Swipe at Tallest Tower in Saudi Capital
articles.content_orig:
Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis hit Saudi Arabian sovereign wealth fund Public Investment Fund Tower on Tuesday, injuring 11.
The kingdom's civil defense directorate did not name the tower, but posted an image showing damage to the PIF tower. Eyewitness reports by Al Jazeera also indicated that the building that was hit was the PIF Tower in Riyadh.
The injured included two Saudi citizens, two Indians, three Nepalis, and four Egyptians.
The attack comes as tensions have flared up again between Saudi Arabia, which is leading an international coalition to restore the internationally recognized government of Yemen after it was forced to flee in 2015, and the Houthis.
Turki al-Maliki , a spokesperson for the coalition, said one of the towers of the financial center was targeted in a "cowardly terrorist attack," referring to the financial center in the Saudi capital of Riyadh.
He added that authorities were conducting an on-site investigation at the scene of the attack.
This has been the second attack by the Iran-backed group in six days on the tower, although the previous attack did not cause any casualties.
On Wednesday, Houthi brigadier general Yahya Saree warned on X that the port of Jeddah and all Saudi ports along the Red Sea coast will become "targets for our forces," if Riyadh attacks the Yemeni Red Sea port of Hodeidah.
The coalition had asked civilians to evacuate the port "for their safety," on Nov. 20.
Attacks by the rebel Houthis have been escalating on Saudi Arabia, with the group targeting one of Saudi Arabia's oil refineries on Sunday , according to Reuters. The Houthis also launched drone and ballistic missiles against the country's airports, most recently targeting the King Khalid International Airport on Oct. 25 , according to reports.
The new attacks come amid wider strikes by Tehran and Iran-linked forces in the Gulf, with Bahrain also reporting that it was attacked by Iran over the weekend. Bahrain is home to the U.S. Navy's Fifth Fleet.
"As a result of the heinous Iranian aggression, a civilian industrial facility was targeted, causing a fire at the site," Bahrain's Ministry of Interior said on X.
The ministry later said two people , a Bahraini citizen and a Pakistani resident, were injured in the attack.
— CNBC's Azhar Sukri contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: See all of Trump’s Nvidia stock trades since January
articles.title_zh: See all of Trump’s Nvidia stock trades since January
articles.content_orig:
SALT LAKE CITY — Utah Sen. John Curtis said he agreed with tech CEO Jensen Huang's initial decision to step down from Nvidia and appeared skeptical about Huang's sudden reinstatement this week.
Huang's surprise comeback as head of one of the world's most prominent chip manufacturers was met with bipartisan pushback. Huang initially left the company after it was revealed he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
President Donald Trump took credit for Huang's return to Nvidia. But the move prompted skepticism from some in Washington, including Curtis.
"Nvidia's board says it relied on input from senior U.S. officials to conclude that bringing Jensen Huang back posed no national security risk," the Republican senator wrote on X. "I have some questions. Who in our government weighed in? What did they tell the board? And on what basis did the board conclude there was no risk?"
He added that Huang's initial decision to leave Nvidia after news of the affair broke was the right call.
"Just 11 days after Nvidia announced his departure, the board brought him back while its own independent investigation was still underway," Curtis continued. "Last week, the board said it didn't intend to reinstate him. I'd like to know what changed."
Meanwhile, Sen. Mike Lee, R-Utah, has been quiet on social media about Huang and the controversy surrounding his role at Nvidia. A spokesperson did not immediately respond Tuesday when asked if Lee had any comment on Huang's reinstatement at the tech company.
Arkansas Sen. Tom Cotton, a Republican who chairs the Senate Intelligence Committee, called for Congress to investigate the situation.
"I have warned the administration from the start about Communist China obtaining our most advanced chips through both smuggling and remote access," he wrote on social media. "The controversy with Nvidia and Megaspeed is just the tip of the iceberg, and it's not resolved because Jensen Huang has his job back."
Megaspeed is a Singapore-based company that is a customer of Nvidia. The alleged spy Huang had an affair with is a former executive for the company.
During a company-wide meeting Tuesday, Huang apologized to employees for making "some terrible mistakes," according to the New York Times , but he challenged the notion that he was back only because Trump pushed for it.
The president's involvement in the issue has raised questions about Nvidia's independence at a time when many are worried about a race with China to develop artificial general intelligence.
"In my opinion, by giving in to Trump, the board is endangering the company," Peter Cohan, associate professor of management practice at Babson College in Massachusetts, told the Associated Press . "That's because Huang has seen that he can do anything he wants, and he will get away with it."
Former Utah Sen. Mitt Romney also weighed in on the latest AI developments on Tuesday, referring to the reported sales of AI chips to China.
"Let me get this straight: we rushed AI along without regulating safeguards in order to stay ahead of China and at the same time, we sold China the very chips they'd need to get ahead of us," Romney wrote on X. "Smells of profit, corruption and perhaps worse."
The U.S. Department of Commerce has approved selling more than 800,000 advanced AI chips to Chinese companies this year, including companies with ties to the Chinese military, the New York Times reported last week. On Sunday, before Huang was renamed CEO, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called for answers about Nvidia's chip sales to China.
"We've been in touch with the temporary management, with the lead directors, with their lawyers, and we do need answers," he told CBS' "Face the Nation."

articles.title_orig: Team Trump Plans New Wave Of US Tariffs, India, China On Hit List: Report
articles.title_zh: Team Trump Plans New Wave Of US Tariffs, India, China On Hit List: Report
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
GUANGZHOU, China — Behind the scenes, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent spent months pushing for action that would signal resolve within the Trump administration against China’s pursuit of the most powerful American computer chips, a flashpoint  in their race for superiority in artificial intelligence, multiple sources said.
But President Trump’s courtship of Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping, seeking to alleviate tensions between the world’s greatest powers, and a contingent of advisors skeptical of commercial warfare against Beijing slowed the process down — giving China months of opportunity to gain access to U.S. semiconductors through the back door.
Ultimately, just hours before departing for Asia alongside  Trump, Bessent got his way, bolstering his position ahead of talks with Chinese officials in Shenzhen this week on the risks posed by frontier systems.
A new rule tightening loopholes in U.S. export controls sends a dual message to Beijing ahead of Thursday’s summit: that Washington is serious about curbing Chinese circumvention — and that China hawks within the administration may be gaining the upper hand.
Trump has repeatedly sidestepped confrontation with Xi over the intensifying AI race in their two previous meetings this year, in Beijing and Washington, wary of upsetting a carefully managed detente and reluctant to jeopardize a technology boom increasingly central to the U.S. economy.
The new rules restrict remote access to advanced U.S. computing chips and servers, marking the latest step to limit China’s abilities to use U.S. chips to train their best AI models.
But the administration, from the president down, is acutely aware of China’s ambitions to dominate an industry that could reshape the global balance of power. That competitive drive was underscored this month by a scandal involving a Chinese espionage campaign targeting Jensen Huang, co-founder of Nvidia, the world’s leading AI chip maker.
Before resigning from the company in disgrace Thursday, Huang admitted to having an affair with a suspected Chinese spy — a woman who worked at a firm in Singapore accused by American authorities of helping to divert restricted Nvidia chips to China, in violation of U.S. export controls.
The national security scandal has roiled the markets — and in so doing, commanded Trump’s attention — inflicting a significant devaluation on Nvidia and reverberating well beyond it, wiping nearly $1 trillion from the combined market value of major technology companies in a single trading session on Monday.
Trump, who counts Huang a friend and ally, indicated he would be open to his return as Nvidia’s chief executive. Bessent suggested otherwise, expressing confidence its board could find competent new leadership and urging a full investigation.
Huang indicated his interest Tuesday in returning to Nvidia, writing in a social media post that “I would be honored” to resume his role as CEO if asked by the board of directors. But Nvidia Chairman Harvey Jones said later Tuesday that the company does not intend to bring Huang back.
Trump is not expected to raise the Nvidia matter directly with Xi. But Bessent plans to do so in his own meetings, one official said.
The Treasury secretary has thus taken on the role of an enforcer, pursuing a tougher line than Trump is willing to take himself in his highly personalized relationship with the Chinese leader.
Bessent is scheduled to meet with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng on the sidelines of the summitry in Shenzhen to discuss potential collaboration on AI safety protocols, standards for testing of advanced models, and a direct communications channel for AI emergencies.
The two men have met before to discuss AI, most recently in New York, where they agreed in principle to coordinate. But the talks have yet to produce much in the way of tangible results.
“Bessent is signaling that, while he sees working with Beijing to mitigate AI risks as a priority, it won’t come at the expense of actions that he sees as necessary to protect U.S. national security, like limiting AI chip exports to China,” said Daniel Remler, a senior fellow with the Technology and National Security Program at the Center for a New American Security.
The administration’s latest action marks a policy defeat for Howard Lutnick , secretary of the Commerce Department, who oversees chip policy and had advocated for a less restrictive approach than Bessent, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Jamieson Greer, the U.S. trade representative.
The feud began spilling into public view ahead of the president’s travel, and in light of the Nvidia scandal, after Bessent said in a television interview that the Commerce Department “has the pen” to act, implying a split within the team.
“Look, there’re two different views,” Trump told reporters Monday, answering questions on the matter. “One view is you don’t want to insult China. We have a very good relationship with China, and you don’t want to insult them.”
“The other view is just go, you know, down and dirty and do what you have to do,” Trump continued. “You can’t say either is wrong or right. We’ll let you know.”
Beyond the diplomatic niceties, Trump has been explicit and consistent since resuming office that the United States must “win” the race for AI superiority, calling the alternative “not acceptable.”
“Whoever wins AI,” Trump said at the United Nations General Assembly in September, “whoever wins superintelligence, wins.”
Trump will arrive in China on Wednesday after meeting with world leaders in Manila, including those from the Quad — an alliance of Japan, India, Australia and the United States —  who discussed AI at their own summit Tuesday evening.
Describing “superintelligence” — Trump’s preferred term for AI — as “the greatest opportunity for economic growth since the Industrial Revolution,” Trump announced a Quad effort to accelerate adoption of the technology, including an investment of more than $85 million to enhance AI ecosystems throughout the region.
“We want to be careful with it,” Trump said, “but it’s amazing, the things that have come out, in terms of science and in terms of medical breakthroughs. No one can believe what we’re finding. And we’re finding it fast.”
“We want to be very careful, but we want to cherish it,” he added. “The United States as you know is leading in that capacity, by quite a bit.”
As he meets with the leaders of India, Japan and Australia, Trump will face pressure to sustain resolve against Beijing despite his yearlong courtship of President Xi Jinping.
The new U.S. rule requires overseas data centers serving customers in China, Russia, Iran and Cuba to identify their end users before gaining access to chips. It also imposes additional licensing requirements on chip sales to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil, which the Commerce Department identifies as posing a “higher-than-normal risk of diversion” to unauthorized destinations.
U.S. officials say that export controls are not up for negotiation in talks with the Chinese. But Beijing sees them as yet another historic example of Washington trying to contain its rise — a posture that has repeatedly stifled diplomatic progress between the two superpowers.
“While administration officials say export controls aren’t up for negotiation, Chinese officials will certainly bring them up,” Remler said. “These restrictions are the key obstacle to China’s AI progress, which is increasingly important to the Chinese economy and to Xi’s strategic goals.”
China claims it does not seek an all-powerful, generalized “superintelligence,” but rather specialized AI systems embedded across industries to boost productivity and improve quality of life.
In Beijing’s telling, it is the United States — pursuing generalized AI through a private sector largely unchecked by the federal gove

articles.title_orig: China investigates politburo star in Xi Jinping’s latest purge
articles.title_zh: China investigates politburo star in Xi Jinping’s latest purge
articles.content_orig:
The Communist Party chief of Shanghai, considered a protege of Chinese leader Xi Jinping, has suddenly been placed under investigation –– marking an escalation of an anti-corruption purge that’s already ensnared a large swath of the country’s top talent .
Chen Jining, 62, who has run China’s largest city and financial center since October 2022, is facing a corruption charge and is suspected of “serious violations of discipline,” state media Xinhua said on Tuesday evening.
It is a stunning downfall for Chen, who was seen as a rising political star and even being mentioned among potential heirs to longtime leader Xi by China watchers.
Xi, who is all but certain to assume a precedent-breaking fourth term in office next year, has executed an unrelenting anti-corruption drive for well over a decade that has brought down senior political, military and judicial figures once thought untouchable. The speed and scale of that effort has reached unseen levels in recent months.
Chen becomes the fourth person from the 24-member politburo –– the top echelon of power in China –– to fall since the last party congress in 2022.
The investigation is being conducted by China’s main anti-corruption body, the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection (CCDI).
Chen’s last public appearance seems to have been on Thursday, November 19, when he inspected the headquarters of a Chinese shipping conglomerate.
Unsurprisingly, government platforms in Shanghai have quickly taken down posts mentioning Chen.
China’s iron fist: Xi Jinping and the stakes for America
Trained as an environmental scientist, the urbane and English-speaking Chen rose through the party ranks in the past two decades. Before moving to Shanghai, he was mayor of Beijing and orchestrated the 2022 Winter Olympics in the capital.
His appointment to the top party job in Shanghai marked a quick elevation. The post usually paves the way for further promotion to the Politburo Standing Committee – the pinnacle of the party’s power structure. Both Xi and China’s former leader Jiang Zemin have followed this path.
It can be lonely at the top. And that’s just how China’s leader likes it
Prior to his Beijing mayoralty, Chen spent over a decade at the Ministry of Environment and Ecology. He also served as the president of Tsinghua University in Beijing, one of China’s most prestigious academic institutions.
After earning a master’s degree in civil and environmental engineering from Tsinghua in the 1980s, Chen went on to study at London’s Imperial College, where he earned a doctorate.
Just in the past two months, Xi’s clampdown on top officials brought the downfall of Beijing’s deputy mayor and a retired former mayor of Chongqing who had withstood several prior political storms.
The party’s top military decision-making body, the usually seven-member Central Military Commission, is now down to only two members with one of those being Xi himself .
Since Xi, 73, came to power over 14 years ago, millions of rank-and-file officials have also been caught in his dragnet.
Between 2012 and 2022, over 500 ministerial-level officials were convicted, removed from their posts, and expelled from the party for corruption, according to official data from the CCDI – with more than 410 officials purged in the last three years alone.

articles.title_orig: US court convicts China’s Huawei for fraud, conspiring to steal trade secrets, in sprawling trial over Iran business
articles.title_zh: US court convicts China’s Huawei for fraud, conspiring to steal trade secrets, in sprawling trial over Iran business
articles.content_orig:
A United States jury has convicted Chinese tech giant Huawei Technologies of conspiracy to steal trade secrets and bank fraud as it grew into one of the world’s biggest suppliers of gear for wireless telecommunications networks.
However, jurors on Tuesday acquitted the company of the most serious charge it faced: engaging in a criminal racketeering conspiracy. The charge is typically used in organised crime and drug cases, but prosecutors used it to accuse Huawei of operating in an illicit fashion to steal intellectual property from US companies.
The verdict followed a lengthy trial in which US prosecutors argued that Huawei repeatedly stole technological secrets from competitors and partners in the US and elsewhere.
Huawei was also accused of doing business in countries subject to US sanctions, including Iran and North Korea, and making false statements to US government officials and banks as part of an effort to hide its misdeeds.
US authorities had targeted Huawei for years, saying the company posed national security risks.
The criminal case began in 2018, and the following year the US government placed Huawei on a trade blacklist that restricted its access to US technology.
Experts have said the case has not undermined Huawei’s business, as the company diversified and emerged as a key player in China’s push for artificial intelligence.
The trial lasted more than two months, with prosecutors calling more than 60 witnesses and the defence calling 15.
Huawei and three affiliates faced 12 charges, including racketeering conspiracy, bank fraud, wire fraud, sanctions violations, and conspiring to steal trade secrets and obstruct justice.
Lawyers for the company said US investigators had used isolated episodes of wrongdoing by a few of Huawei’s more than 200,000 employees to spin a false narrative about a grand conspiracy that did not actually exist.
Huawei lawyer Brian Heberlig said the company would appeal the convictions but saw the racketeering conspiracy acquittal as vindication.
“That was the only count that brought all of the allegations together,” and the jury rejected it, he said outside court, saying that the verdict “repudiated the central government narrative in the case”.
It is unclear what effect the verdict might have on Huawei’s global fortunes. The company hasn’t been allowed to sell equipment to US carriers for years because of security concerns. It has also been blacklisted by other Western allies, including Canada and the United Kingdom.
The case emerged in December 2018 when Meng Wanzhou, Huawei’s chief financial officer and daughter of the company’s founder, was detained in Canada on a US warrant, prompting a diplomatic crisis involving the US, China and Canada.
Meng had been secretly indicted for allegedly misleading an HSBC banker about Huawei’s business in Iran, so the company could move dollars in and out of Iran in violation of US sanctions.
She fought extradition to the US for nearly three years, before entering a deferred prosecution agreement and flying home to China to a hero’s welcome. The charges against her were dropped.
The 2018 indictment alleged that Huawei misled HSBC, Standard Chartered and BNP Paribas about its business dealings in Iran.
Prosecutors added new charges in 2020, including that Huawei conspired to steal trade secrets from US technology companies over two decades.
During the trial, prosecutors tried to prove Huawei stole source code from Cisco Systems for its routers, stole wireless telecommunications company Quintel’s antenna technology, and hired a professor to gain access to a circuit board developed by semiconductor company CNEX.
Jurors watched a video that, according to prosecutors, showed a Huawei employee slipping a piece of a T-Mobile testing robot into his backpack, and heard about a Huawei engineer sneaking into a Fujitsu booth at a trade show to photograph a device.
Prosecutors gave jurors a statement attached to Meng’s deferred prosecution agreement, in which she acknowledged that the company illegally conducted business in Iran. She did not testify at trial, though an HSBC banker she met with in 2013 did testify.
The defence argued that HSBC and the other banks knew about Huawei’s business in Iran and were competing for Huawei’s business.
Heberlig accused prosecutors during his closing argument of having “cherry-picked” a handful of disparate incidents to support their claim of a 20-year conspiracy.
He said Huawei succeeded through “hard work, innovation, and investment in research and development”.
Huawei has more than 200,000 employees and operates in approximately 170 countries.

articles.title_orig: US ready to slap tariffs on China, EU and others over subsidized production, AP sources say
articles.title_zh: US ready to slap tariffs on China, EU and others over subsidized production, AP sources say
articles.content_orig:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Trump administration is expected to soon announce plans to raise tariffs on China, the European Union and 14 other economies, according to two people familiar with the matter.
The U.S. Trade Representative's Office is expected to release the results of a monthslong tariff investigation into the industrial subsidies by the 16 economies in the coming days, according to the people who were not authorized to comment publicly and spoke on the condition of anonymity.
They stressed the timing for the rollout of the tariffs could still change. The White House and USTR did not respond to requests for comment.
Plans for the new tariffs are part of an effort to replace broader duties the administration set last year that were subsequently struck down by the Supreme Court. The plans were reported earlier on Tuesday by Bloomberg and The Wall Street Journal.
The tariffs are in response to what the White House has said is excessive manufacturing output in those countries, boosted by subsidies, that has led to a flood of goods at lower prices that undercut American companies.
The anticipated action constitutes a second step in the administration’s efforts to replace the duties announced in April 2025 that the Supreme Court ruled unconstitutional in February. The White House slapped 60 trading partners with levies of 10% to 12.5% in July, charging that they have inadequately enforced bans on goods produced by forced labor.
The anticipated trade action demonstrates that the Trump administration is still willing to impose import taxes despite a sweeping loss for the Republican Party in this month’s midterm elections, fueled largely by affordability concerns as inflation remains elevated. At the same time, the new duties could test how the Democrats will respond to tariffs imposed unilaterally by Trump.
Even with majorities in both the House and Senate, Trump could veto any legislation that overturns or waters down the tariffs.

articles.title_orig: Russia's own figures show almost 500,000 deaths in war in Ukraine
articles.title_zh: Russia's own figures show almost 500,000 deaths in war in Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
At least 490,334 Russian soldiers have died since the start of the war in Ukraine in 2022, according to Russian government statistics analysed by the BBC.
The leaked Rosstat data reveal how the full-scale invasion of Ukraine has fundamentally changed mortality patterns in Russia, and show the high cost paid in human life in a war that Vladimir Putin had assumed would last only days but is now almost five years old.
BBC Russian has had access to more than 11 million death records from 2021 to September 2026, after a hack by Belarusian group Cyber Partisans BY and Ukraine's Silent Crow.
Russia's statistics agency admitted to a cyber-attack, but denied any protected information had been leaked.
Together with independent Russian outlet Mediazona, BBC Russian has compared the Rosstat data with its own list of confirmed military deaths, pulled from open sources since the start of the invasion, and it has found matches for 90% of the records.
The records show that 65% of 18 to 24 year-olds in Russia who lost their lives in 2025 died in the war. For those aged 25-34 the number was 59%. Only among 45 to 54 year-olds does cardiovascular disease claim more Russian lives than the conflict.
The data also reveal the extent of losses in specific areas of Ukraine. Some 20,000 Russian soldiers died fighting for control of 10 Ukrainian villages whose combined pre-war population was 12,000.
During the fight for one small village called Andriivka, south of the town of Bakhmut in Donetsk region, 1,122 Russians lost their lives. Before the war 74 people lived there.
Russia does not give public figures for losses sustained since the war began in February 2022. And two years ago Rosstat stopped publishing data of deaths from external causes, which was used to gauge the extent of military losses.
For example, only 70% of deaths we have established of soldiers from the occupied regions of Donetsk and Luhansk in eastern Ukraine who fought in the Russian army  were accounted for in the Rosstat files.
The Rosstat dataset contains no names but does include ages, places of residence, places of death and also circumstances of death.
We have filtered the records first by location, leaving only Ukraine as well as Russian border regions that saw incursions by the Ukrainian army.
Next, we identified 425,174 entries explicitly indicating a military-related cause of death, such as explosions or shrapnel during combat operations.
As this count could include civilians, we filtered out women as well as men outside the 18-65 age group. And if someone lived and died in the four Ukrainian regions occupied by Russia, we excluded them as a possible civilian – unless he had a record of military service attached to his entry.
Another 14,093 entries were identified by looking at employment, and 51,067 were recorded in the database as deceased on the basis of a court ruling. This often happens when a soldier goes missing in a combat zone for more than six months and their body has not been recovered.
Again, we filtered out civilians by only counting deaths in the war zones in Ukraine and Russia.
BBC Russian's own detailed records of Russian losses has reached 290,012, verified together with Mediazona from official reports, social media, new memorials and graves. The actual death toll is likely to be higher, as not all deaths are reported publicly.
Overall, the Rosstat dataset confirms the trends that we have observed with our own count.
According to BBC Russian's analysis of the leaked files, in the first year of the war the average age of those killed was 34. By 2025, as prisoners and contract soldiers entered the ranks, it had risen to 40 (38 according to our own list).
Some of Russia's poorest regions in Eastern Siberia account for a disproportionately large share of the losses. Men from Tyva, Buryatia and Zabaykalsky Krai are 20-25 times more likely to die in the war than residents of the biggest cities of Moscow and St Petersburg.
In most regions, the distribution of deaths based on Rosstat data differs from that in the BBC's list by just a few tenths of a percentage point.
At least 5,017 foreigners are among those who died fighting for Russia, according to our analysis of the Rosstat files, including 1,031 Uzbeks and 720 Tajiks. We have left out Ukrainians from this count to avoid including civilians.
This is a conservative estimate as dual nationals are listed as Russians in the database, and there is no reference to North Koreans who died repelling the Ukrainian incursion into Russia in 2024.
The BBC identified 2,304 North Korean soldiers who died there by analysing satellite imagery and official photographs of a newly built memorial in Pyongyang.
The leaked Russian statistics may not be complete but taken in conjunction with BBC Russian's own work they are significant. Military experts estimate that the BBC's figure of 290,012, gleaned from open sources, may account for 45-55% of the true death toll – ranging from 527,295 to 644,471.
In the context of a war that has lasted four years and 10 months, these are high numbers for Russia, when compared with the Soviet war in Afghanistan that ended in 1989.
Ukrainian losses were last put at about 50,000 by President Volodymyr Zelensky in July 2026, but another list based on open sources by the anonymous UA Losses website puts the figure at 115,952.
Additional reporting by Ilya Barabanov

articles.content_orig:
SALT LAKE CITY — Utah Sen. John Curtis said he agreed with tech CEO Jensen Huang's initial decision to step down from Nvidia and appeared skeptical about Huang's sudden reinstatement this week.
Huang's surprise comeback as head of one of the world's most prominent chip manufacturers was met with bipartisan pushback. Huang initially left the company after it was revealed he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
President Donald Trump took credit for Huang's return to Nvidia. But the move prompted skepticism from some in Washington, including Curtis.
"Nvidia's board says it relied on input from senior U.S. officials to conclude that bringing Jensen Huang back posed no national security risk," the Republican senator wrote on X. "I have some questions. Who in our government weighed in? What did they tell the board? And on what basis did the board conclude there was no risk?"
He added that Huang's initial decision to leave Nvidia after news of the affair broke was the right call.
"Just 11 days after Nvidia announced his departure, the board brought him back while its own independent investigation was still underway," Curtis continued. "Last week, the board said it didn't intend to reinstate him. I'd like to know what changed."
Meanwhile, Sen. Mike Lee, R-Utah, has been quiet on social media about Huang and the controversy surrounding his role at Nvidia. A spokesperson did not immediately respond Tuesday when asked if Lee had any comment on Huang's reinstatement at the tech company.
Arkansas Sen. Tom Cotton, a Republican who chairs the Senate Intelligence Committee, called for Congress to investigate the situation.
"I have warned the administration from the start about Communist China obtaining our most advanced chips through both smuggling and remote access," he wrote on social media. "The controversy with Nvidia and Megaspeed is just the tip of the iceberg, and it's not resolved because Jensen Huang has his job back."
Megaspeed is a Singapore-based company that is a customer of Nvidia. The alleged spy Huang had an affair with is a former executive for the company.
During a company-wide meeting Tuesday, Huang apologized to employees for making "some terrible mistakes," according to the New York Times , but he challenged the notion that he was back only because Trump pushed for it.
The president's involvement in the issue has raised questions about Nvidia's independence at a time when many are worried about a race with China to develop artificial general intelligence.
"In my opinion, by giving in to Trump, the board is endangering the company," Peter Cohan, associate professor of management practice at Babson College in Massachusetts, told the Associated Press . "That's because Huang has seen that he can do anything he wants, and he will get away with it."
Former Utah Sen. Mitt Romney also weighed in on the latest AI developments on Tuesday, referring to the reported sales of AI chips to China.
"Let me get this straight: we rushed AI along without regulating safeguards in order to stay ahead of China and at the same time, we sold China the very chips they'd need to get ahead of us," Romney wrote on X. "Smells of profit, corruption and perhaps worse."
The U.S. Department of Commerce has approved selling more than 800,000 advanced AI chips to Chinese companies this year, including companies with ties to the Chinese military, the New York Times reported last week. On Sunday, before Huang was renamed CEO, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called for answers about Nvidia's chip sales to China.
"We've been in touch with the temporary management, with the lead directors, with their lawyers, and we do need answers," he told CBS' "Face the Nation."

articles.title_orig: Jim Cramer sizes up six retail stocks after earnings — and names his two favorites
articles.title_zh: Jim Cramer sizes up six retail stocks after earnings — and names his two favorites
articles.content_orig:
CNBC's Jim Cramer on Tuesday assessed the latest earnings reports from six major retailers, identifying which stocks have more room to run.
Retail stocks have been a bright spot the last few months as investors rotated out of technology stocks and oil prices and interest rates retreated from their highs. The SPDR S&P Retail ETF (XRT) has gained 9% this quarter, while the Technology Select Sector SPDR ETF (XLK) has plunged nearly 20% and the S&P 500 has shed almost 6%.
"Retailer earnings went great today, with all six major retailers that I was watching gaining ground, and several — including Dollar Tree, Dick's, Kohl's and Abercrombie & Fitch — notching strong double-digit gains," the " Mad Money " host said.
"That said, some reports were better than others," he added. "Burlington Stores and Kohl's basically just beat low expectations, Dick's had a nice bounce-back quarter, and Dollar Tree was very solid. But Best Buy and Abercrombie & Fitch, two of our favorite names in the group, had the best reports of all."
Here's where Cramer stands on each retailer.
Dollar Tree shares surged 11% after the discount retailer beat expectations for comparable sales, revenue and adjusted earnings per share and raised its full-year outlook. "This is a company that's been focused on self-help initiatives recently, and the combination of their progress on that front and the value proposition they can offer ... are driving the strong performance that we've seen from Dollar Tree recently," he said.
Burlington Stores missed comparable sales and revenue expectations while merely matching earnings estimates. Cramer attributed Tuesday's 4% rally to low expectations following a more than 30% decline from its all-time closing high on July 30, as well as the company's largely unchanged fourth-quarter outlook. He still prefers TJX Companies , which delivered a much stronger report last week , and is a holding in Cramer's Charitable Trust .
Dick's Sporting Goods shares jumped almost 15% after the retailer beat on top and bottom lines and raised its full-year earnings outlook. Despite inventory challenges across the athletic footwear and apparel industry, Cramer said Dick's is "controlling what it can control, taking market share while the market is muted, and setting itself up for long-term success."
Best Buy delivered "arguably the best set of numbers from any retailer that reported" despite posting the smallest stock gain of just 3%, Cramer said. Comparable sales rose more than 6%, and the electronics retailer also raised its full-year outlook, projecting comparable sales growth of 2% to 4% for the holiday quarter.
Cramer attributed the muted stock reaction to Best Buy's nearly 80% rally from its 52-week closing low on May 13. "At less than 15 times earnings, with a 3.9% yield and this latest quarter nearly for free, I think Best Buy is still a buy," he said.
Kohl's shares climbed 19% after the department store chain beat comparable sales and earnings expectations, though tariff refunds contributed significantly to the bottom-line beat. Like Burlington, Kohl's benefited from low expectations.
"Kohl's is a funky story," he said. "Credit to them for not doing as badly as the analysts expected them to. But it's still not a business that I'm a long-term believer in."
Abercrombie & Fitch shares surged almost 20% after the apparel retailer topped expectations and raised its full-year outlook. Cramer praised the company's disciplined inventory management, which has supported pricing power and margins.
"ANF can be a boom or bust stock, but right now it's booming, and I don't think it's done going higher," Cramer said.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia's Jensen Huang still has security clearance, sources say
articles.title_zh: Nvidia's Jensen Huang still has security clearance, sources say
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang still holds a security clearance, multiple sources familiar with the matter told CBS News.
Huang has drawn weeks of scrutiny , following reports that he had an affair with a businesswoman and alleged Chinese intelligence asset whose company is suspected of transferring advanced Nvidia chips to China. Huang resigned as Nvidia's chief executive two weeks ago, but the company's board reinstated him on Monday following direct appeals from President Trump, who said he offered the board an "assurance" that Huang did not pose a national security threat.
Revoking Huang's clearance was discussed, sources said.
Huang never received a defensive security briefing from the administration after he was alerted about businesswoman Alice Huang's alleged ties to China, a source directly familiar with the matter said. Such briefings, also called counterintelligence briefings, help people with a U.S. government security clearance recognize threats.
It is not uncommon for executives at tech companies that do classified federal work to have security clearances.
Earlier Tuesday, Attorney General Todd Blanche told reporters he wasn't sure whether Huang still held a security clearance. He did not offer any specific findings on Huang, and didn't say whether federal investigators interviewed Huang or examined his relationship with an alleged spy.
Blanche said the government relies on a "collective consensus" among federal agencies to assess national security risks and determine whether somebody is able to access sensitive government information.
An Nvidia spokesperson declined to comment on Huang's clearance.
In an interview on CNBC Monday, Mr. Trump broadly defended Huang, saying a "very thorough investigation" found he "did nothing wrong," aside from "bad judgment having to do with somewhat unrelated incidents."
Asked what Blanche had told him about the situation, Mr. Trump said: "They did a pretty good investigation, and they felt that he himself was exonerated."
The Justice Department has overseen a criminal investigation into Megaspeed , after the Commerce Department looked into whether Megaspeed had violated export control rules, both agencies confirmed last week. The status of that probe is unclear.
Asked whether the Justice Department investigated Jensen Huang before Mr. Trump assured Nvidia's board that he had not engaged in wrongdoing, Blanche said he would have informed the president if the department had evidence Huang had committed a crime.
"To the extent that that Department of Justice had information that he was committing crimes or something like this … that's something that I would have certainly told the president had it been true," Blanche said.
Pressed on how the department could rule out potential criminal liability while export-control investigations remained ongoing, Blanche said he could not predict whether future investigations might produce different findings.
"I can't predict the future," Blanche said.
Blanche also described Nvidia as "a good corporate citizen," saying he had no reason to suggest the company was obstructing a federal investigation.
Asked whether Huang's reported relationship with someone allegedly connected to Chinese intelligence presented a national security risk, Blanche said officials must rely on actual intelligence assessments rather than news accounts.
"I don't deal in leaks or in the public reporting that's in some newspaper," Blanche said. "We have to deal with actual facts and what the intelligence community has actually said, which is not something that we should be sharing with the media. And so my personal view of that question is completely irrelevant."

articles.title_orig: I Designed My Dream Ferrari 296 Challenge Stradale. It's Ridiculous
articles.title_zh: I Designed My Dream Ferrari 296 Challenge Stradale. It's Ridiculous
articles.content_orig:
Ferrari’s new 296 Challenge Stradale is a badass, 670-horsepower, non-hybrid race car for the road. Want one? It’ll cost you around $307,000 before options.
But if you want to get a little fancier with your new Ferrari, the automaker’s online configurator has plenty of ways to customize the supercar. And some of them are pretty wild. I wasted 30 minutes of my day dialing in my perfect 296 CS.
Let’s start with the most important part: paint. Ferrari offers a whopping 35 colors, split into four categories: Standard, Historical, Classic, and Special. You could go with the classic Rosso Corsa or Giallo Modena, but I'm going with something a little different here: Giallo Ambra, aka fancy orange.
Once you pick your paint, Ferrari lets you choose from a handful of livery options, including upper- and lower-body graphics, wing decals, door numbers, and more. Normally, I'd say a livery is mandatory on a car like this. But the 296 Challenge Stradale looks so damn good in a single color that it really doesn't need one.
Ferrari also lets you turn just about anything into carbon fiber. Front splitter? Carbon fiber. Rear diffuser? Carbon fiber. Even the engine covers? That's right, carbon fiber.
If you really want to go crazy, you can replace all the glass with Lexan, a lightweight polycarbonate that's a little lighter than traditional glass. That should help shave off a few pounds. Ferrari will even let you ditch the Prancing Horse badges on the front fenders entirely or swap the metal logos for painted ones.
Ferrari offers six wheel designs for the 296 CS, ranging from light silver to darker gray and black. You can also customize the wheel bolts, center caps, and more. I'm going with Forged Diamond-Polished wheels and titanium wheel bolts.
Depending on how you plan to use your 296 (primarily on road or track), Ferrari offers both Bridgestone and Pirelli tires. There are even two Pirelli "Color Edition" options with yellow or gray accents. We'll pass on those.
Brake calipers are available in eight different colors, ranging from black and red to yellow and silver.
Most of the interior upgrades are pretty subtle. You can choose floor mats with or without logos, pick from 26 stitching colors (we went with Filo Spec Flash Orange to match the exterior), and customize the lower portion of the dashboard with 22 different colors.
Perhaps the most important choice, though, is the seats. Ferrari offers two options: Racing and "Best Weight," as the automaker calls it. The racing seats appear to be lighter and probably less comfortable, but Ferrari doesn't really divulge any specifics.
There are seven different Alcantara colors available, depending on which seats you choose. You can also customize the seatbelts with six different colors, add a central racing stripe, and choose from additional stitching options.
Like most Ferraris, the 296 CS doesn't have a dedicated center touchscreen. That said, Ferrari does offer an optional passenger display, which seems a little odd in a car like this. Maybe your nephew can watch Shrek while you lap COTA. The world is your oyster.
As you'd expect, Ferrari doesn't list prices for any of these options in its configurator. You'll have to contact your local dealer to find out how much any of them will set you back.
But getting into a new 296 Challenge Stradale will cost you at least $307,000 to start. And that's before you start checking boxes.
