articles.title_orig: Blanche Downplays Questions Over Nvidia as Investigators Examine Company’s Customers
articles.title_zh: Blanche Downplays Questions Over Nvidia as Investigators Examine Company’s Customers
articles.content_orig:
US Attorney General Todd Blanche has backed Nvidia as a "good corporate citizen" while refusing to comment on whether the AI chipmaker was under federal investigation.
Blanche said he had no information about newly reinstated CEO Jensen Huang's security clearance status, as lawmakers demand answers about President Donald Trump's involvement in Huang's comeback.
Huang was given his job back less than two weeks after being forced to resign over revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.
Asked several times on Tuesday if the justice department or FBI had investigated Huang, Blanche responded: "I don't know what you're talking about."
Huang is still set to appear before Congress next week, where he will be questioned about national security concerns over his relationship with an alleged China spy who led Megaspeed,  a Singapore-based corporate customer of Nvidia.
The US commerce department has also announced it was preparing to blacklist the tech company Megaspeed, which has been suspected of helping to divert advanced chips to China.
In a joint statement last week, the commerce and justice departments said they began investigating Megaspeed in 2024 "for potential export control violations" .
But speaking to reporters on Tuesday, Blanche said the latter department has "hundreds, if not more" export investigations occurring at any one time.
"So when you say the export investigation is still ongoing, I don't know what you're talking about," he said.
Asked if he was satisfied Nvidia had been co-operative with any efforts to get to the bottom of whether the company or Huang potentially knew about any chips being diverted to China, Blanche said: "I have no reason to stand up here and say Nvidia is anything but a good corporate citizen.
"Obviously, if Nvidia was the target or was subject to some criminal investigation or they were obstructing or thwarting our investigation, then that wouldn't be the message that the president is saying to the American people.
"It shouldn't be what my message would be either."
While Nvidia's stock market value surged on the announcement of Huang's reappointment, some of the gains were reversed in volatile Tuesday trading.
The company's share price closed down nearly 6% - still well above where it ended last week. On Monday, Nvidia stock rocketed more than 31% following news of Huang's return.
The company's board reinstated Huang on Monday in a shock U-turn. Harvey Jones, chairman of Nvidia's board, said Huang's return was in the "best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers".
The board said it had received input from senior levels of the US government and was confident that Huang's reinstatement posed no national security risk.
On Monday, Trump said he spoke to the company's directors and convinced them to bring back Huang .
Huang's reinstatement provoked bipartisan anger.
Republican congressman Don Bacon said Nvidia should have "ignored the Administration's inexplicable desire to save Huang".
Republican Senator Pete Ricketts said Huang's behaviour "doesn't absolve Nvidia of answering for national security concerns and unaccounted-for chips".
Democratic congressman Robert Garcia, the incoming chairman of the House oversight committee, said Trump's "direct involvement" with Nvidia's decision "raises serious national security and corruption questions".
Democratic Senator Ruben Gallego said Congress needed to "investigate what stock positions took place before the announcement".

articles.title_orig: Stock Market Today: Tech Stocks Slide Back After Epic Rally
articles.title_zh: Stock Market Today: Tech Stocks Slide Back After Epic Rally
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Nvidia's ( NVDA ) stock fell 7% on Tuesday, reversing from a strong 31% rally on Monday, after the company's board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO.
In a statement, the board said it had a series of discussions with Huang and was satisfied with his candor and ability to lead the company. "The board believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers," Nvidia chair Harvey Jones said. Jones will remain the chair of Nvidia's board.
In an interview on Monday, President Trump said he had spoken "directly and indirectly" with the board and "convinced" them to make a deal. Top administration officials also reportedly assured the Nvidia board that Huang wasn't a national security risk and wasn't facing alleged chip-smuggling charges.
"I am honored to return to Nvidia and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution," Huang said in a statement.
The New York Times reported on Tuesday that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang apologized to employees during an hourlong, companywide meeting, stating that his actions were "not acceptable" and violated Nvidia's code of conduct. Huang also said that he was in therapy.
"I made some terrible mistakes," Huang said, per the Times. "I was unfaithful to Lori, and I hurt my kids, and of course, I hurt all of you."
Huang, however, pushed back against the notion that he was a "tech bro" and above the code of conduct.
He also said his return wasn't the result of the board caving to pressure from President Trump. "That is completely untrue," Huang reportedly said, claiming instead that the board "gathered facts" — including that the DOJ didn't consider him a national security threat — and evaluated whether he deserved a second chance.
Rep. Gregory Meeks, a ranking member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee and New York Democrat, called on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to testify at a public hearing for the House, adding another request for Huang to answer questions on Capitol Hill.
Huang is already scheduled for a transcribed interview with Meeks and the committee chairman, Rep. Brian Mast, next week. Huang is also confirmed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next week.
"Americans deserve answers to the profound questions that are continuing to emerge about NVIDIA and our national security," Meeks wrote. "President Trump's intervention to reinstate Jensen Huang as NVIDIA's CEO raises even more concerning questions about the administration's own role, questions the American people deserve to hear answered in public."
President Trump's full-throated support for Jensen Huang and his reinstatement atop Nvidia ( NVDA ) has not been matched by Republican lawmakers, who say they intend to keep the pressure on the chipmaker.
The objections broadly fall into three categories. A handful of Republicans say it was a mistake to reinstate Huang as CEO. Another group says they have serious concerns and feel that US national security has been compromised. And a third group says simply that they have unanswered questions about the whole affair.
According to a Yahoo Finance tally, a majority of the 13 Republican senators whom Huang will face next week on the Senate Banking Committee have offered at least a promise of tough questions, and two members have even said Huang should not be in the CEO chair.
North Dakota Republican Kevin Cramer recently posted that the legal cloud was "risk enough to not rehire Huang," while Nebraska's Pete Ricketts said his "behavior does not support reinstatement." Both will have time to question Huang.
The hearing will be overseen by Chair Tim Scott of South Carolina, who said in his own statement that national security will be "central to the committee's oversight."
Nvidia's board undermined its claims of independence by reinstating CEO Jensen Huang before investigations into his conduct concluded, investors and corporate governance experts said on Monday.
The decision is striking because the board effectively vouched for Huang's candor and fitness to lead the company before its own investigation was complete, raising doubts ‌about whether directors had sufficient information to make an independent judgment, these people said.
Nvidia said on Monday that after talks with senior US officials, its board "is confident that Mr. Huang's reinstatement poses no ‌national security risk."
… The situation undercuts the board's standing, said New York City Comptroller Mark Levine, who helps manage retirement funds that hold some 5 million Nvidia shares.
"They told us flatly that he would not be coming back. They have done a total 180 without any explanation, or any indication that concerns about ‌legal and other liabilities have been resolved," Levine said in a telephone ⁠interview.
"They have proven they're not independent, and that is the defining quality that we need from any board," he said.
Nvidia stock is bouncing off its session lows, but shares remain down over 7% as the chipmaking giant gives back some of its gains made on Monday.
The broader chip sector faced selling pressure as investors rotated out of tech and assessed the implications of Jensen Huang's return as CEO and the market's massive rally the day before.
This price reflects trading activity during the overnight session on the Blue Ocean ATS, available 8 PM to 4 AM ET, Sunday through Thursday, when regular markets are closed.
A Department of Justice official said that President Trump spoke with Attorney General Todd Blanche over the weekend and that the DOJ had no evidence of any wrongdoing by Jensen Huang or Nvidia.
In an interview with CNBC on Monday, Trump stated that Nvidia asked "for assurance on the national security threat."
"And we gave them assurances at least with everything we know. And we know a lot," Trump said Monday.
Seaport Research Partners senior analyst Jay Goldberg weighed on Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia, telling Yahoo Finance that it was "probably the least bad option for Nvidia."
Still, he noted, "a lot of the issues that I talked about a month ago before we had all of this drama, still exist, right? There are still real questions about their growth prospects and their reliance on some questionable sales to Asia and their their questionable financing deals across the industry. So I certainly still have a lot of questions."
Watch the interview below:
When it comes to the AI trade, this has been the year of AMD ( AMD ). AMD's stock has sizzled, up 112% year to date compared to an 11.5% drop for its top rival Nvidia.
As Nvidia's ( NVDA ) founder Jensen Huang has been embroiled in scandal and the tech trade has been pressured, AMD shares have hung tough. The stock is down 12.2% over the past month versus a 22% decline for Nvidia.
The biggest question for AMD right now is this: Does Huang's stunning return as CEO of Nvidia mean bad news for AMD in 2027 and beyond?
Pros think AMD will be just fine, for now.
"I don't see how this changes it completely," Moor Insights & Strategy founder Patrick Moorhead said on Sozzi Unleashed . "I was saying early on when Jensen left that nothing changes for 18 months. And the reason is the supply chain is locked, the wafers are locked, data center configurations are locked around Nvidia design. So nothing would change, I think, if Jensen had been removed permanently."
Colette Kress has been the CFO of Nvidia ( NVDA ) since 2013, helping to build the company at the center of the AI boom alongside founder and public face Jensen Huang. She stepped into the line of fire for 12 days as interim CEO while Huang worked behind the scenes to return.
She withstood fresh reports of Huang berating her in meetings, and President Trump saying in an interview that she did a poor job in her post-earnings TV interview last week.

articles.title_orig: Utah asks to drop charges against Kalshi and its founders after Kalshi halts trading there
articles.title_zh: Utah asks to drop charges against Kalshi and its founders after Kalshi halts trading there
articles.content_orig:
Utah on Tuesday dismissed criminal charges against Kalshi and its two co-founders following the decision by the prediction market platform on Monday to suspend operations in the state.
The state originally filed the 14 criminal charges against the company and founders Tarek Mansour and Luana Lopes Lara on Oct. 28, claiming that Kalshi operated an illegal gambling operation in the state.
The Commodity Futures Trading Commission — the federal regulator for prediction markets which views itself as the sole body that can develop rules over the growing industry — sued Utah the day before the state announced its charges.
Mansour and Lara were slated to appear in a Utah district court on Dec. 4, according to court documents.
However, Kalshi suspended operations in Utah on Monday, citing legal uncertainty. Utah Attorney General Derek Brown celebrated the decision in a statement announcing the move to dismiss the state's charges.
"Every company in this space should take note," he said. "If they promote, support, or enable gambling, we will hold them accountable."
Brown's office noted in the statement that dismissal is without prejudice, meaning if Kalshi were to begin operations again in the state the charges could be refiled.
"Good faith jurisdictional disagreements should never be criminalized," Kalshi's general counsel Yaakov Roth said in a post on X . "We stand ready to work with State AGs on reasonable interim measures until courts resolve the dispute over who regulates prediction markets."
While Kalshi faces legal setbacks in Utah, it faced some relief in New York on Monday when a state judge denied an emergency temporary restraining order against the company to halt its operations in the jurisdiction . The court will hear arguments on the matter again in January.

articles.title_orig: China-linked network using AI fakes to smear Taiwan election candidates, BBC Verify finds
articles.title_zh: China-linked network using AI fakes to smear Taiwan election candidates, BBC Verify finds
articles.content_orig:
Taiwan's ruling party is being repeatedly targeted with AI videos spreading false claims about its leader and other key members ahead of crucial local elections, BBC Verify has found.
A China-linked network has pumped out more than 500 fake videos about the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) in the past year, which experts suggest is part of a long-running campaign to influence the outcome of the elections.
The videos appear to try to smear President Lai Ching-te by claiming he holds a US green card - and would abandon Taiwan if war broke out with China - which Taiwan's presidential office says is completely false. Deepfakes also appear to show Puma Shen, who is running to be the mayor of capital Taipei, using drugs, which he denies. Others seek to undermine or ridicule the politicians by showing them in children's clothing or as popular film characters.
The Taipei mayoralty has traditionally served as a springboard to the presidency. Experts say this has made Shen, who has been openly critical of Beijing, an obvious target for disinformation campaigns. The current mayor, Chiang Wan-an, is part of Taiwan's Kuomintang (KMT) party, which favours closer ties with China.
Taiwan is a self-governing island that China claims as part of its territory. Beijing and Taipei have long observed an uneasy status quo under which Taiwan, backed by the US, neither formally declares independence nor unites with China.
But tensions have risen since the DPP came to power in 2016. Beijing has repeatedly accused the party of pursuing independence while China's leader Xi Jinping, who has said "reunification" with Taiwan is a key goal, has stepped up pressure against the party with increased military activity around the island.
Experts believe the current disinformation activity is part of a broader campaign against Taiwan designed to undermine trust in its democratic process.
"The account operators are trying to make people distrust the DPP politicians so that they will not believe whatever they say," Austin Horng-En Wang, an expert in cognitive warfare at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas, told BBC Verify. "If you don't trust that candidate then you will not listen to what they say," he added.
The videos, many of which were shared from an account called "noxparable" or carried a watermark with the same name, have been viewed tens of millions of times across several social media platforms since May 2025.
More than half of those views were tracked in the past four months as the activity has ramped up ahead of the elections. Many of the accounts involved in spreading disinformation listed their locations on social media as mainland China and Hong Kong, while a number of the clips carried labels showing they were generated with AI. Many people who engaged with the videos were often seen repeating the false claims or attacking DPP figures in the comments, while others appeared to treat the clips as entertainment.
One of the most widely shared videos targeted Shen by superimposing his face onto a man who is seen holding a lighter and exhaling smoke alongside claims he is smoking drugs. The video appears to build on accusations from Taiwan's opposition party that he supports drugs decriminalisation, which Shen denies, and was debunked by a local news network.
Shen has taken legal action against people sharing deepfakes, local media reported, while his campaign office said AI videos showing the candidate appeared to be part of a "classic tactic China uses to smear specific targets". BBC Verify contacted the Chinese embassy in London for comment.
Other debunked claims include allegations that Lai's predecessor Tsai Ing-wen had fraudulently obtained her PhD from the London School of Economics. The university pushed back on identical allegations in 2019 and confirmed it had awarded her the doctorate.
A number of the social media accounts BBC Verify identified as sharing the disinformation videos appeared to be linked to Chinese firm Borderless, which produces websites that blend apolitical content with pro-China messaging. The network has also been investigated by journalists at the Taiwanese independent media outlet The Reporter, who shared their findings with BBC Verify. Borderless has previously been accused of carrying out "cognitive warfare" against Taiwan by Taipei's National Security Bureau and the firm has been contacted for comment.
Analysts confirmed to BBC Verify there were also linguistic clues that the accounts, which presented themselves as based in Taiwan, were actually posting from China. The posts occasionally used a simplified Chinese script introduced by the Communist government which was never adopted in Taiwan.
The posts mostly appeared during regular office hours, which Wang suggested showed a "professional" operation, while the accounts originating outside Taiwan showed evidence of election interfering. "When they pretended to be citizens in another country and used these accounts to manipulate the public opinion of the other country during the campaign, it is definitely election interference," Wang added.
Earlier this month, Taiwan's central election commission aired an advert warning voters to "beware of AI-generated deepfake videos" circulating online that could seek to influence the upcoming election. It comes as government officials flagged nearly 2,700 social media accounts to Meta that it claimed were part of a Chinese information warfare campaign, Reuters reported. Meta said it had removed the accounts.
Andrew Yeh of the China Strategic Risk Institute said the ultimate goal is not to favour any party. "China's information operations succeed not just by backing one candidate or opposing another, but by diluting Taiwan's policy debates, driving polarisation and degrading Taiwanese citizens' trust in their democratic processes," he said.
"Regardless of whether the KMT or DPP comes out on top, a more fractured and more divided Taiwan is in Beijing's interests."

articles.title_orig: These North Koreans say they were spied on, beaten and jailed for being Christian
articles.title_zh: These North Koreans say they were spied on, beaten and jailed for being Christian
articles.content_orig:
Living in North Korea, Kim Bo-bin got used to praying with her eyes open.
She found ingenious ways to keep her Christian faith a secret in the Communist dictatorship, which tightly controls how and where its citizens worship. Unauthorised displays of faith could land people in prison, she tells the BBC.
So Kim would silently mouth hymns and clap with just two of her fingers. "In North Korea, if there are three people in a room, you are being spied on. So I would only close my eyes [and pray] when I lay on the floor."
Now 44, Kim lives just outside the South Korean capital Seoul, where she fled 15 years ago.
Her testimony - of how she prayed in secret for years, and was jailed and beaten for her faith - is part of a new report documenting the experiences of 570 North Korean escapees, most of whom say they experienced or witnessed anti-Christian persecution.
Spanning five years and featuring interviews with defectors from across the country, the report by British human rights group Korea Future accuses Kim Jong Un's regime of repeatedly violating religious freedom through a system of surveillance, fear and violence. It suggests little has changed after sustained international pressure, with multiple incidents of suspected Christians being beaten and tortured as recently as last year.
North Korea maintains that it allows religious freedom in spite of years of evidence heard by rights groups and the United Nations. While churches exist in Pyongyang, they are controlled by the state and widely seen as projecting an illusion of religious liberty.
"The North Korean leader's authority is god-like," says Kang Dong-wan, professor at Dong-a University. "So they cannot allow gods whose authority is above him." Pyongyang fears that religious freedom may threaten the regime itself,  he adds.
First established in Korea in the late 1700s, Christianity exploded across the north after Protestant missionaries arrived in the 1880s. North Korea provides no figures on its Christian population but the UN has referred to estimates of 200,000 to 400,000 of them practising secretly, some of whom are detained in camps.
Surveillance and control over religion, like many other aspects of North Korean life, intensified under Kim Jong Un, who succeeded his father in 2011.
Three South Korean missionaries operating in the Chinese border region were arrested between 2013-2014 and sentenced to life in prison on charges of espionage and plotting a coup. It's not clear if they are still alive, as Seoul says Pyongyang has refused to share any information about the detainees.
Pyongyang has also been cracking down on smuggled memory sticks containing South Korean-made videos of Christian sermons. In 2020, it passed a law - on Rejecting Reactionary Ideology and Culture - to block so-called "foreign influence". Owning Bibles and hosting services can now result in imprisonment, while distributing religious books or videos is punishable by death.
Lessons against religion begin as early as kindergarten for most North Koreans. Children must attend "self-criticism" sessions at school in which they are warned against "superstitions", widely understood to refer to Christianity and other faiths.
This is what Kim Bo-bin recalls being taught. The faiths Koreans have long practised - Christianity since the 18th Century and shamanism, a millennia-old practice rooted in ancestral spirit worship - were dismissed as superstitions.
Her teachers never mentioned that Kim Il Sung himself was born into a fervently Christian family, or that Pyongyang had once been dubbed the "Jerusalem of the East."
Rather, every child and adult is expected to know North Korea's foundational Ten Principles by heart. They state that citizens must hold the "firm perspective" they know of "nothing greater than the great comrades" Kim Il Sung, the founder of North Korea, his son Kim Jong Il and the ruling party. The "smallest attempt" to dent this authority must not be tolerated, it adds.
The report documents both the indoctrination as well as the constant surveillance, with police and a network of neighbourhood spies monitoring suspicious activities. A former police informant says she was instructed to gather information on neighbours' worshipping, and handed a memo by an officer describing Christianity as an "anti-socialist activity".
North Korean authorities are also reported to hold intergenerational records of families' beliefs condemning Christians' children and grandchildren to a life without higher education or decent career prospects.
All of this illustrates how various North Korean institutions, including schools and the police, control its citizens' beliefs from "cradle to the grave," co-author James Burt says.
And yet many North Koreans turn to religion because their lives are so precarious, he adds. Faith offers them something that the state ideology "with its rigid doctrines and disconnect from their lived realities" cannot.
Kim Bo-bin grew up in North Hamgyong province, along the border with China. It was a remote, impoverished part of the country where those deemed "untrustworthy" by the state ended up, such as landowners and Christians.
Stuck at the bottom of a state-enforced hierarchy, this "hostile class" had little chance of moving up the ladder. Many of Kim's neighbours were barred from higher education and government positions, or ever living in Pyongyang.
One of them was an exiled "crazy grandma" who used to disappear into a coal shed every morning to chant words 10-year-old Kim didn't recognise. "One day, [the grandma] told me we go from ashes to ashes and dust to dust," she recalls. It was only 12 years later, when she encountered a Bible for the first time in her life that she realised the grandma was a Christian.
When a devastating famine began in the late 1990s, North Hamgyong was one of the first regions to starve because it was cut off from the state's food supply which prioritised Pyongyang. Millions were killed in what the regime described euphemistically as the "Arduous March". It was a time when many North Koreans crossed into China seeking food and work.
Kim was one of them. Aged 22 in 2003, she took what she believed was a job opportunity in China offered by a friend's aunt. But once she crossed the border, she was forced into marriage with a Chinese man and became pregnant.
While picking up a free pram for her newborn daughter at a building adorned with a cross, she encountered a missionary for the first time. Kim would join a growing group of people who discovered Christianity in China - a group that Pyongyang saw as a threat when they were returned to the North, according to Prof Kang.
Kim was arrested in China in 2007 and deported. During interrogation, she says North Korean secret police asked her if she'd ever worn a cross on her neck. She pretended not to understand. She told the police she only recognised the symbol from hospital buildings.
Kim Bo-bin says it was God's blessing the interrogator seemed more interested in whether she intended to flee to South Korea, a grave offence. She says she was beaten for 23 days and sentenced to three years of hard labour at a prison. Her story tallies with multiple accounts in Korea Future's report of extreme police violence causing broken bones and severe bleeding.
Lee Young-joo, who Kim Bo-bin met in prison also after being deported from China, tells the BBC she was interrogated about whether she'd met any missionaries, been to a church or seen a Bible. "Of course you must deny all of it. I said no, I haven't seen it," she told them.
In her prison cell, Lee says she'd keep her eyes open, begging God to save her life. Whenever anyone shut their eyes, guards would swear and shout: "Are you praying?"
Lee is glad she wasn't found to be a Christian, because she says she "would have been sent to a political prisoners' camp. I would be tortured and never allowed to leave and be buried there." This is a widely-held fear among defectors, although Korea Futu

articles.title_orig: Colette Kress Scored a Win Worth Millions From Huang’s Return to Nvidia
articles.title_zh: Colette Kress Scored a Win Worth Millions From Huang’s Return to Nvidia
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia finance chief Colette Kress led the company for 11 days during Jensen Huang's sudden but brief departure. When Nvidia's board officially reinstated Huang as CEO on Monday, the company also announced that Kress would continue in her role as CFO.
The 59-year-old Kress currently has roughly 4.775 million shares directly and indirectly held, which makes her worth approximately $778 million at Monday's market close.
The 63-year-old Huang resigned earlier this month following revelations of extramarital relationships, including one involving an alleged Chinese spy.
Nvidia stock soared 31% and the Nasdaq surged more than 6% Monday after the company announced that Huang would return as CEO, president and board director, effective immediately. Huang returned to the office Monday to crowds of Nvidia employees cheering his return .
Kress, who stepped in as interim CEO during Nvidia's moment of crisis, joined the chipmaker as finance chief in September 2013 following stints at Cisco, Microsoft and Texas Instruments.
As CFO, Kress oversees the balance sheet of a company aggressively financing many of the infrastructure deals that power the artificial intelligence buildout. Those agreements also raise concerns over circular financing and Nvidia's AI exposure in the event of a slowdown.
In the first earnings call after Huang's resignation, Kress sought to reassure investors, raising the company's fiscal 2028 revenue-growth forecast to roughly 75% from 70%.
She told analysts during a Q&A portion that it was "business as usual" at the company. She later told CNBC's Jim Cramer that customers have stood by the chipmaker and that demand continues increasing.
"The board has determined that they will not reinstate Jensen, and that is our statement and what the board has decided to do," Kress said.
During the company's first all-hands meeting after Huang's resignation, Kress also struck an optimistic tone , telling employees to "move forward" and mentioning pay raises.
But Kress didn't manage to impress many market participants and insiders, who compared the interim chief to Huang. Last week, the stock recorded its worst week and longest weekly losing streak since the 2008 financial crisis as AI stocks plummeted.
"She just wasn't him," The Futurum Group CEO Daniel Newman told CNBC. "I think she would have had to strengthen her bench around her a lot, because you have a visionary, product technology driven CEO that was literally the epicenter of the company. He was the entire identity."
One person CNBC spoke with said Kress handled the situation with "skill and grace" while managing a tough job.
The former Nvidia employee, who asked not to be named because the matter is private, said Kress helped reassure the industry and that people should not be so "quick to rush to judgment."
In the week since Huang's exit, The Wall Street Journal reported that Huang belittled Kress, calling her "a deer in the headlights."
Huang said in the press release announcing his return that he was "grateful" for Kress "leading NVIDIA during this period."
"I think she is a fantastic CFO. I think Jensen probably has great confidence in her. I hope she stays," the former Nvidia employee said. "I don't think that she's going to be on thin ice when Jensen returns."
Nvidia did not immediately respond to comment for this story.

articles.title_orig: After my divorce, I started taking myself on solo dates to nice restaurants. I don't need a partner to feel special.
articles.title_zh: After my divorce, I started taking myself on solo dates to nice restaurants. I don't need a partner to feel special.
articles.content_orig:
I lived well while abroad, often buying myself flowers and indulging in moments of whimsy.
When I moved back to the US, I realized I stopped dating myself, and my life felt a bit boring.
Now I book solo trips and dine at fancy restaurants alone. I don't need a partner to feel special.
It was Valentine's Day, and I was ferociously clicking at my laptop in a metal music brewery in Denver, trying, of all things, to book a ticket to see the NYC Ballet performance of "The Sleeping Beauty" in a few days.
A few hours prior, I had gotten not what I'd call a breakup text per se, but rather a "we shouldn't keep getting to know each other" message.
In all fairness, we lived three time zones apart and were about a decade apart in age . It was in that moment that I could see why he felt compelled to make that choice. Since moving back stateside a few months prior, I had gotten a bit complacent in romanticizing my life in the same way I did during my time in London. And dare I say, had become a bit boring.
Whether it was taking myself to a West End show or spoiling myself with arms full of bouquets from Columbia Road Flower Market , I had grown accustomed to treating myself to regular moments of whimsy.
The author, shown in Mdina, said she's no longer waiting for celebratory occasions to make herself feel special.Courtesy of Jen Kaarlo.
After separating from my husband a decade prior, I was no longer waiting for celebratory occasions to make myself feel special. It's not as if I woke up one morning and decided to take myself on a divorce-moon to Oman (which I did, too), but like any relationship — romantic, platonic, or otherwise — it really blooms when there are moments of surprise and delight sandwiched in between the day-to-day. Only now, it was on me to create those moments for myself, so I did.
Why should we reserve occasions to feel special for a current or future TBD partner, when we could instead relish in showing up as a cool, sexy date for ourselves?
I love spending time with my people, be it my two dads, my best friends, and plenty of people in between, but I also learned a long time ago that you can't wait on others' availability to do the things that make your heart sing.
So, in that moment, with my phone and the "it's not you, it's me" text in my hands, I canceled my day of errands, went somewhere new, and started booking a last-minute trip to New York as if I were going to sweep myself off my own feet. A bit ridiculous, I know, but I'm thrilled I did.
Then, as if I had a fairy godmother pulling the strings backstage, everything fell into place. I managed to snag a ridiculous deal at The Langham for a room, one of the last available seats at The New York City Ballet, and a reservation at the just-opened Marcel for dinner.
The author said she enjoyed her solo trip to New York and that it gave her a bit of her sparkle back.Courtesy of Jen Kaarlo.
I packed my most sequined pieces and set off to The Big Apple to reignite my sparkle . And while I got unexpectedly stuck in New York because of the blizzard, the trip did the trick of bringing back a burst of color to a life I had started seeing as a bit dull.
There are so many excuses to stay home, save money, avoid the hassle of travel, but I think that's exactly why it's important not to. I've learned that it's important to break up the monotony of adulting and to remember to fall back in love with your life from time to time. I've found that when you start reintroducing that joy back into your life, it's almost as if you remember that magic and possibility do, in fact, exist.
At this point, I'm well-versed in solo travel and love taking myself out to romantic restaurants and asking for a table for one. (The Grotto Restaurant in Malta being one of my faves.) While some people glare over, most couldn't be bothered, and in the grand scheme of things, why should it matter? I'm likely never going to run into them again anyway. Instead, I get to relish in my party for one and know I'm not letting the magic of life pass me by.
If you enjoyed this story, be sure to follow Business Insider on Yahoo.

articles.title_orig: Nuclear test veterans will get full truth, says Burnham, as he confirms independent panel
articles.title_zh: Nuclear test veterans will get full truth, says Burnham, as he confirms independent panel
articles.content_orig:
Andy Burnham has told nuclear test veterans they will get "the full truth" as he confirmed plans for an investigation into the health legacy of Britain's Cold War-era atomic programme.
The prime minister has ordered an independent panel modelled on the Hillsborough disaster investigation to assess the potential impact of testing exercises in the 1950s and 1960s.
Burnham told veterans and their families that the government would treat the process with the "utmost seriousness" as he vowed to set up a "gold standard" investigation.
The Ministry of Defence (MoD) has for decades denied it covered up the impact of radiation on troops ordered to carry out nuclear weapons tests.
A BBC Newsnight special programme heard reaction from veterans, including John Morris, a laundry operator at a nuclear test site who went on to develop cancer and lost a four-month-old son. He believes both were linked to radiation exposure.
He said: "Seventy-two years ago I was an 18-year-old, sent to Christmas Island, totally unaware of what I was being led into.
"I am here today and I am looking for, and sincerely hope we will get, justice."
Veterans who were involved in the tests, predominantly carried out in Australia and the South Pacific, have long called for a full investigation into the long-term health effects it had on them and their children.
Many of the surviving veterans say they were more likely to develop a range of illnesses in the years that followed, while their descendants say they have suffered an increased risk of hereditary illnesses and fertility problems.
Veterans have recounted being ordered to fly through radioactive clouds without protection, witnessing atomic explosions with nothing to shield them from the fallout, and living on sand they believe was contaminated with nuclear material.
The announcement of an independent panel is the culmination of years of campaigning by the LABRATS group and others, and comes 14 years after a legal challenge at the UK Supreme Court failed.
Many veterans have died in the decades since the tests, but some of those still alive shared their stories with Newsnight on Tuesday.
Brian Unthank says he witnessed three hydrogen bomb explosions in the Pacific without protective equipment and went to on develop multiple skin cancers.
He said: "I've always wanted to get a prime minister... to stand up in Parliament and make a total, abject apology for the total mess-up of the way they treated us veterans and the families through this 74 years.
"Next year is our 75th year of misery. Let's get it done today."
Barbara Quick, whose father served in the RAF Police on Christmas Island - a major site for UK and US nuclear testing in the Pacific Ocean - told BBC Newsnight she had never been able to have children and two of her sister's children had died. She blames health complications arising from their father's exposure to radiation.
She said: "If you were higher personnel you got the gas mask, you got the suit - but my father was told to turn his collar up, turn his back and cover his eyes."
Steve Purse, whose father was a nuclear test veteran, was born with complex disabilities he says have never been fully diagnosed. He told BBC Newsnight the announcement was "huge" but that the panel must be allowed to provide full disclosure.
He said: "No-one has listened to us like this before, it's a moment of history."
Before becoming prime minister earlier this year, Burnham told BBC Newsnight the nuclear veterans had been subjected to a "criminal cover-up on an industrial scale" and backed calls for an investigation.
On Tuesday, he told campaigners at Downing Street: "All I can say is you know the courage you've shown, the dignity you've shown through the whole thing, given everything that happened, is honestly something that we just are in awe of.
"Your patience, your strength, your determination - and we will make sure that this process moves as quickly as possible to get you what you long deserved, which is the full truth... Obviously, I do not know what the full truth will be, but we will get it."
The MoD has previously said four studies found no increased health risks for those involved with the tests, as did a study carried out by Brunel University in 2022.
However, campaigners and veterans have accused the MoD of withholding full health records, including blood and urine tests, which they say would establish a link.
The MoD released some official documents in July 2026 , though it said some records may have been inadvertently destroyed three years earlier.
The department also said the medical records that veterans and their families were trying to access would appear "complex and inconsistent" as a central database was never held by the military, in part due to the intense Cold War-era security around the nuclear tests.
The independent panel announced on Tuesday will be be modelled on the Hillsborough Independent Panel and chaired by the same person, James Jones, the former Bishop of Liverpool.
He told BBC Newsnight: "The nuclear veterans have for decades made serious allegations against the state about what happened to them and to their descendants through the exposure to nuclear radiation. These merit serious investigation."
Downing Street said it would produce a report by October 2027 to coincide with the 75th anniversary of the first British nuclear weapons test.
Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said: "It's taken too long to get here and I think today of the people who haven't lived to see this moment - and I fear for the people who might not see the outcome."
He acknowledged low trust in the MoD among veterans and their families, assuring them the department would not be involved with setting up the panel or defining its remit.
He said the panel would "help us to make sure that the cover-up is exposed".
Asked if the government would pay compensation should the panel recommend it, Streeting said he would not pre-judge its report but that he felt "absolutely sure the findings will be uncomfortable" and the government "will have to take that on the chin".

articles.title_orig: Microsoft’s historic cloud outage exposed an engineering “fog of war”
articles.title_zh: Microsoft’s historic cloud outage exposed an engineering “fog of war”
articles.content_orig:
According to internal memos reviewed by Reuters , Microsoft has declared a “Code Red” overhaul of its engineering response practices after the November 12 outage that lost access to Exchange Online, Teams, and Outlook for users worldwide.
Per the memos, Microsoft 365 Core President Jason Henderson described the outage as having the most customer impact in the history of Exchange Online. In a separate memo, Henderson wrote that an urgent production fix in a recent incident took five to six days to reach worldwide saturation. Microsoft’s target for its most urgent security fixes is to move from detection to safe worldwide deployment in one hour. “Needless to say, we aren’t here yet,” Henderson wrote.
The memos, which Reuters reviewed but Microsoft has not published, outline the response to the November 12 disruption. The company’s post-incident report , dated November 20, attributed the downtime to an undetected Windows scalability defect introduced in July, which caused lock contention in the gateway processes. A Teams traffic failover then dumped additional load onto infrastructure already under stress, as maintenance had left nearly 14 percent of gateway server capacity offline at the time of the incident.
Amanda Silver , a corporate vice president overseeing Microsoft 365 Core and Work IQ, wrote that engineers had to contend with a “fog of war” as the outage unfolded. According to Silver, responders exchanged more than 11,000 messages across 11 Teams chats, leaving diagnostic data scattered, and a full view of the incident fractured. Silver’s memo also quotes Charles Lamanna, executive vice president of Copilot, Agents and Platform, telling a Code Red review that the affected component had accumulated “roughly ten years’ worth of acceptable failures.”
Microsoft has said the outage was not related to any cyberattack or malicious activity, and the defects were not caused by AI tooling.  As part of the Code Red overhaul, Silver’s memo outlines five workstreams focused on load shedding, geographic traffic partitioning, and faster recovery mechanisms. According to Reuters, Microsoft plans to improve its incident response and patching timelines by deploying its own AI agents to help engineers diagnose system health data more quickly. Henderson said that he will hold daily meetings with the Substrate leadership team, which oversees the engineering team responsible for Microsoft 365 services.
Microsoft has set targets of one-hour worldwide resolution in major incidents and a one-hour deployment window for urgent security fixes. It hasn’t said when it hopes to meet them, or how future response efforts will avoid 11 separate Teams chats and the “fog of war.”

articles.title_orig: Amazon customers may qualify for $309.5M settlement. See how
articles.title_zh: Amazon customers may qualify for $309.5M settlement. See how
articles.content_orig:
Amazon customers who experienced issues with returns or refunds over a nearly nine-year span may be eligible for a share of a $309.5 million class-action settlement . But some shoppers must act soon to receive a payment.
The deadline to submit a claim is Dec. 1 for customers who qualify under one of the settlement's two groups. Other eligible customers will receive payments automatically if the agreement receives final court approval.
The settlement stems from a lawsuit alleging that Amazon's return policies and practices violated Washington consumer protection and other laws. The allegations involve customers who did not receive refunds for returned products, received incorrect or delayed refunds, or were charged again after receiving a refund.
Amazon denies the allegations and any wrongdoing.
Here is what customers should know about eligibility, filing a claim and how much money they could receive.
Customers may qualify if they initiated a return or requested a refund for a physical product purchased through Amazon.com and received in the United States between Sept. 5, 2017, and Feb. 12, 2026.
To qualify, customers must have experienced at least one of the following:
It depends on which settlement group a customer belongs to.
Subclass A: Customers in this group do not need to submit a claim form. However, they must select their preferred payment method through the official settlement website within 105 days after the court grants final approval.
Subclass B: Customers in this group must submit an eligible claim form to receive compensation. Claims can be submitted online through the settlement website or by mailing a completed form to the settlement administrator.
The deadline to submit a claim is Dec. 1. Mailed claims must be postmarked by that date.
Customers who are unsure whether they qualify can contact the settlement administrator at 1-888-553-4246.
The settlement includes a fund of $309.5 million, which will be distributed among eligible customers after court-approved expenses, attorney fees and other costs are deducted.
According to the settlement terms, 92.7% of the net settlement fund is allocated to Subclass A members, while 7.3% is allocated to Subclass B members.
Individual payments will depend on the value of customers' eligible unpaid transactions and a proportional amount for potential prejudgment interest. The settlement does not specify a fixed payment amount for each customer.
Payments will be distributed after the settlement receives final court approval. The process could take additional time if appeals are filed.
A final approval hearing is scheduled for March 16, 2027, at 10 a.m. PT in the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Washington in Seattle.
The court will determine whether the settlement is fair and should receive final approval. No payments will be distributed unless the court approves the agreement and it becomes final.

articles.title_orig: Shein to pay $100 million to settle federal claims that it deceived U.S. customers
articles.title_zh: Shein to pay $100 million to settle federal claims that it deceived U.S. customers
articles.content_orig:
Shein has agreed to pay $100 million to settle allegations that the fast-fashion company harmed consumers by misleading them about its products and policies.
The Federal Trade Commission alleges that the Singapore-based retailer made it hard for customers to resolve purchase problems, broke its shipping promises, suppressed negative reviews and engaged in other deceptive practices.
"Shein attracted consumers with promises of affordable clothing, fast delivery and use of suppliers that earned above-average ratings on standards related to child and forced labor, among other representations,"  Christopher Mufarrige, director of the FTC's Bureau of Consumer Protection, said in a statement on Tuesday. "In reality, the company misled millions of consumers about its products, its suppliers and the authenticity of its customer reviews. Shein further compounded consumer harm by making it extraordinarily difficult to obtain customer service."
Shein, which ships roughly 1 million packages to the U.S. daily, employed only five customer service representatives to field calls from American consumers about their orders, according to the FTC.
Shein also made deceptive claims about its supply chain and the origin of its cotton and failed to provide customers with shipping updates or help them locate late or missing packages, the agency alleged in its complaint .
The $100 million will be used to provide redress to Shein customers, the FTC said. Under the agency's proposed order, Shein is also barred from making misleading claims about shipping and delivery times and from suppressing negative product reviews. The company is also required to provide adequate customer service.
A Shein spokesperson said the agreement "does not constitute an admission of liability, and we continue to disagree with aspects of the FTC's characterization of our business and compliance practices."
Shein went public on the Hong Kong exchange in September. It's built a sizable customer base in the U.S., appealing to shoppers with ultra-cheap clothing styles and fast delivery.
Last year, the White House ended the "de minimis" tariff exemption that allowed low-cost packages, including shipments from Shein, to enter the U.S. duty-free. In April, Shein said it would raise prices for consumers after the loophole closed.
The Associated  Press contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia live updates: Nvidia stock falls after massive rally, Jensen Huang apologizes to employees
articles.title_zh: Nvidia live updates: Nvidia stock falls after massive rally, Jensen Huang apologizes to employees
articles.content_orig:
Jensen Huang is back as the CEO of Nvidia , and is now tasked with selling the company's artificial intelligence vision while also defending himself in Washington.
As Nvidia employees celebrated the return of their leader to the company's headquarters, Huang told the gathered crowd, "I'll be a better CEO the second time around."
Huang will need to be a better CEO to head off the issues surrounding Nvidia and the broader AI industry exposed by Huang's exit. The challenges include a proliferating roster of investigations and hearings from Congress, regulators and state-level officials , as well as technical and competitive questions about how long Nvidia's currently dominant graphics processing units can remain on top.
"There's nothing prohibiting him from doing what he does on his day job," said Katten chair and former federal prosecutor Gil Soffer. But investigations take significant prep time, Soffer said. "You don't just walk in cold."
At Nvidia's GTC conference in Washington, D.C., next week, the company will attempt to convince customers, partners and suppliers that it is developing the future of AI. At the same time, lawmakers will be pressing its newly reinstated CEO over what he knew and when about Megaspeed executive Alice Huang .
Huang, before his scandals, was scheduled to give the GTC DC keynote speech on Dec. 1 to discuss new Nvidia products and the trajectory of the AI ecosystem. In the past, the two-hour speech was the highlight of the event with hordes of fans full of the Huang-inspired "Jensanity."
"People will want to see that it's business as usual, which hopefully for Nvidia shareholders will mean that Jensen Huang announces some new exciting products," said Babson College associate professor Peter Cohan.
Right now, Nvidia has Ian Buck, vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing, filling the slot. A representative for Nvidia declined to answer multiple questions about whether Huang would appear at the company's event.
On the same day, Huang is scheduled to speak with three House committees — Foreign Affairs, Select Committee on the CCP, and the Select Committee on Intelligence — behind closed doors, where his interview will be transcribed.
"The NVIDIA board's brief internal investigation and reinstatement of Jensen Huang do not erase the national security threats and questions that must be addressed," the chairs said in a joint statement. They said that Huang has confirmed he will appear for the transcribed interview on Dec. 1.
Next Tuesday's interviews are just the first of a slew of investigations.
On Dec. 3, just as Nvidia's conference is wrapping up, the Senate Banking Committee will hold a hearing titled "Protecting America's AI Advantage: Oversight of U.S. Export Controls." Sen. Tim Scott, R-S.C., who chairs the committee, said Huang will publicly testify as the sole witness.
California's attorney general is also investigating Huang's remarks, and politicians from the Senate Finance, Intelligence, and Foreign Relations committees have inquired about the scandal. In the House, Energy and Commerce has requested a company briefing from Nvidia, in addition to the three committees mentioned earlier. That's not counting an investigation from the Department of Justice and a reported investigation from the Securities and Exchange Commission .
Plus, Huang still has to cooperate with an investigation from the board of directors, led by the law firm Wachtell Lipton.
Meanwhile, Nvidia needs Huang to reassure investors and the broader AI ecosystem that the company is developing new products that will be in high demand. Investors had said that while Nvidia's products for the next two years have been fully designed, they were worried that the chipmaker's pace of innovation would slow without Huang.
Nvidia is facing new competition from chips from its biggest customers, including OpenAI , Anthropic , Google , Amazon and Microsoft . The companies have been developing their own chips to reduce reliance on Nvidia, as well as to control AI costs.
"There was already this worry that we're spending too much on it," said Stephanie Balaouras, vice president of group research at Forrester. "One of those cost management strategies is to match ... the workload requirements to the right infrastructure. You don't need to put everything on a Nvidia GPU."
Many in the AI industry see Huang as one of the staunchest defenders of "open-source" AI that is free to use for commercial purposes, as compared with "frontier models" from companies like Anthropic and OpenAI, which charge users by the token.
Nvidia has also been spending heavily to develop its own open-source models called Nemotron. Currently, Nvidia Vice President Kari Briski is scheduled to present new Nemotron technology at GTC.
On Monday, Nvidia's board said that "senior levels" of the U.S. government provided input on Huang's potential national security risk. President Donald Trump told CNBC that he was central to convincing Nvidia's board to reinstate Huang and said he gave the board assurances.
Trump's help could draw even more scrutiny from Democratic lawmakers, who were already focused on probing Nvidia's chip sales.
"Today's news that Donald Trump engineered the rehiring of Jensen Huang at Nvidia is Exhibit A about the political corruption and rot at the heart of the Trump administration's big tech and AI policy," said Democratic Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland in a call with reporters Monday.
Republicans have also criticized Huang's return as the focus on the company's China sales intensifies. Still, the investigations could start to weigh on Nvidia's CEO, experts say.
"How could he possibly do the job?" Jeff Sonnenfeld , senior associate dean at the Yale School of Management, told CNBC, citing Senate investigations, House investigations and other state investigations, even before Democrats take over next year.
And the reaction in Washington to Huang's scandal could start to affect Nvidia's sales.
Last week, the Department of Commerce announced that it will prevent Chinese companies from getting around export controls by renting Nvidia's chips across borders. On Monday, Commerce also added Megaspeed to a trade blacklist.
And it's not just Nvidia that is relying on a strong performance from Huang. The company's investors, customers, partners and shareholders will also look to see if Nvidia still wants to be at the center of the AI ecosystem. Before Huang was removed, he pushed Nvidia to invest in AI startups, while selling them products, and helping finance their infrastructure.
Remarks from Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress last week while she was interim CEO suggested that Nvidia would be taking a "very strong look" at using its balance sheet to support the AI ecosystem, but it's unclear if Huang's second stint as CEO will continue with his prior showmanship or abide by a more measured approach.

articles.title_orig: Beverly Hills plastic surgeon branded ‘magician’ over dramatic transformation of 61-year-old mom after $45K facelift
articles.title_zh: Beverly Hills plastic surgeon branded ‘magician’ over dramatic transformation of 61-year-old mom after $45K facelift
articles.content_orig:
Beauty is in the eye of the beholder.
But it seems that everyone was blown away by one woman’s recent facelift transformation .
Dr. Marc Levin, a facial plastic surgeon in Beverly Hills , specializes in “dramatic yet undetectable facial rejuvenation.”
The biggest news, opinion and culture shaping California right now.
The expert, 30, who became one of the youngest board-certified surgeons in North America, regularly shares images of his patients before and after their procedures.
Most recently, he uploaded snapshots of 61-year-old hairdresser Helen, who underwent a grueling nine-and-a-half-hour surgery — and the results left the internet stunned.
Dr. Levin shared in the caption of the post: “What a transformation! Absolutely no stone was left unturned for Helen. Every millimeter of her face was analyzed and appropriately addressed.”
He explained how her “character and beauty still remain,” adding: “She is just a younger-looking, more refreshed and clean version of herself.”
Speaking to the California Post, Dr. Levin dished further details about Helen’s “comprehensive facial rejuvenation plan,” which came with a $45,000 price tag.
The extensive list of procedures included an extended deep-plane face and neck lift, endoscopic brow lift, upper blepharoplasty, scarless lower blepharoplasty, facial fat grafting, CO2 laser and an earlobe reduction.
“I’m kind of a younger surgeon so I’m doing the most modern innovations, facial rejuvenation techniques and facelifting techniques,” he told The Post.
And his craftsmanship did not go unnoticed by social media users who flooded to the comments to offer praise.
“Absolutely beautiful… you are so talented and skilled,” one wrote, as another added: “Well, dang…that is a fabulous result!”
Others were quick to brand the surgeon a “magician” and “miracle worker” after seeing the finished results.
In a separate video, Helen, who is originally from South Africa, offered insight on how the procedure had changed her entire outlook.
She began by explaining that she had been “miserable” before taking the plunge to get surgery.
“I looked at the outside of myself and I thought, ‘Oh my God, what is happening to me over here?’ It didn’t match how I was feeling on the inside,” the mom said.
But now, three months post-surgery, she has found a new lease of life.
“I feel like I look like my daughter [now],” Helen revealed, adding: “Thank you for giving me the gift of confidence back.
“How fortunate am I to have the best and most caring surgeon. I’m just so grateful,” she concluded.
Dr. Levin explained that patients will start to see settled results within two to three weeks after surgery.
During this short time frame, “you are able to go out and nobody should know that you had surgery if you have your hair down and makeup on.”
He shared that patients would see their “final results” within three to four months, but will “continuously look better and better for 10 to 12 months after surgery.”

articles.title_orig: Live storm updates: Record king tides leave Bay Area roads flooded
articles.title_zh: Live storm updates: Record king tides leave Bay Area roads flooded
articles.content_orig:
Dangerous high tides, waves reaching up to 30 feet and an incoming storm are expected to bring flooding, heavy rain and strong winds to parts of Northern California this week, threatening coastal communities with road closures, erosion and dangerous beach conditions. The National Weather Service said Tuesday that coastal flooding could reach major to extreme levels in some areas as unusually high tides combine with storm-driven ocean surges.
LIVE: Track rain in San Francisco Bay Area with Live Doppler 7
Low-lying coastal areas could see flooded roads, road closures and erosion. Rising water and waves could also reach farther up beaches than usual, leaving people with fewer ways to escape.
Meanwhile, a cold front is forecast to bring moderate to heavy rain and gusty winds from Tuesday evening into Wednesday morning.
Coastal flood warnings will remain in effect in several areas through Wednesday and Thursday, depending on location.

Powerful king tides pushed San Francisco water levels above 8 feet on Tuesday morning, breaking a previous record for November set in 1982, the National Weather Service said.
At 10:06 a.m. Tuesday, the tidal gauge at Crissy Field near the Presidio was measured at 8.23 feet. The previous record was 7.97 feet on Nov 30 1982. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's tidal records for San Francisco date back to June 29, 1854.
More records could be set Wednesday morning, when the highest tides are expected, according to the weather service.
At the San Francisco tide gauge, water levels could reach 8.5 feet, or 2.7 feet above normal, at 10:49 a.m. In Monterey, tides could rise to 8.4 feet, or 3 feet above normal, at 9:39 a.m., forecasters said.
Early Tuesday, the weather service said that coastal flooding could reach major to extreme levels in some areas as unusually high tides combine with storm-driven ocean surges.
The City of San Francisco has released a storm and flood hazard map that shows which areas are prone to flooding as the region gears up for record king tides.
The city is warning that high tides can flood low-lying Bay streets Wednesday morning even without rain.
The highest tides of the year flooded streets, overflowed docks and submerged sidewalks across the Bay Area on Tuesday, prompting concerns about more coastal flooding to come.
High tide reached many Bay Area communities Tuesday morning.
Along San Francisco's Embarcadero, SKY7 footage showed water beginning to overflow barriers and flow onto nearby sidewalks and streets.
Flooding also submerged many locations across Marin County, where officials made last-minute preparations to protect Highway 101 ahead of the peak tides.
Officials said keeping the highway open would be considered a success as tide levels were forecast to reach 8 feet, with the potential to rise as high as 9.5 feet.
They said mitigation efforts performed well during Monday's high tide and expressed confidence in their ability to manage the higher water levels expected Tuesday.
In Sausalito, king tides flooded low-lying areas along Bridgeway and the Marinship district, turning parts of the city into rivers.
The flooding left some drivers navigating through standing water, while others used kayaks and paddle boards in inundated areas. A Coastal Flood Warning remained in effect.
The king tides are coinciding with a fast-moving rainstorm Tuesday night, and wednesday is expected to see even higher tides.
Several major airlines are preemptively bracing for impact ahead of forecasted storms by issuing waivers for some ticketed travelers during the busy Thanksgiving holiday week.
With storms projected from coast to coast and concerns about potential flooding in San Francisco, a number of carriers issued travel waivers for passengers flying in and out of San Francisco on Wednesday.

articles.title_zh: Hostages held in Cartagena, Colombia, supermarket after failed armored car hijacking
articles.content_orig:
BOGOTA, Colombia — A group of armed men with their faces covered seized a supermarket in the Colombian city of Cartagena on Tuesday and are holding an unknown number of hostages, Colombian police said.
President Abelardo de la Espriella said that the men were “common criminals” who fled into the supermarket after a failed attempt to hold up an armored truck.
The hostage situation broke out as Colombia is experiencing a wave of attacks by rebel groups on government targets, which has recently spread to urban areas.
Footage shared on social media showed dozens of people rushing out of the Exito supermarket, which is located in a mall in Cartagena’s La Castellana neighborhood, while local media have broadcast images of snipers on nearby buildings in what appears to be a standoff between the armed men and police.
Cartagena is one of Colombia’s main tourist destinations. The city of a million people is famous for its well preserved 18th century architecture, and the thick stone walls built to defend it from pirate attacks.
Cartagena’s airport temporarily suspended its operations on Tuesday following the incident. But it later said in an X message that operations were slowly returning to normal.

articles.title_orig: US attorney general dodges questions about Nvidia investigation
articles.title_zh: US attorney general dodges questions about Nvidia investigation
articles.content_orig:
US Attorney General Todd Blanche has backed Nvidia as a "good corporate citizen" while refusing to comment on whether the AI chipmaker was under federal investigation.
Blanche said he had no information about newly reinstated CEO Jensen Huang's security clearance status, as lawmakers demand answers about President Donald Trump's involvement in Huang's comeback.
Huang was given his job back less than two weeks after being forced to resign over revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.
Asked several times on Tuesday if the justice department or FBI had investigated Huang, Blanche responded: "I don't know what you're talking about."
Huang is still set to appear before Congress next week, where he will be questioned about national security concerns over his relationship with an alleged China spy who led Megaspeed,  a Singapore-based corporate customer of Nvidia.
The US commerce department has also announced it was preparing to blacklist the tech company Megaspeed, which has been suspected of helping to divert advanced chips to China.
In a joint statement last week, the commerce and justice departments said they began investigating Megaspeed in 2024 "for potential export control violations" .
But speaking to reporters on Tuesday, Blanche said the latter department has "hundreds, if not more" export investigations occurring at any one time.
"So when you say the export investigation is still ongoing, I don't know what you're talking about," he said.
Asked if he was satisfied Nvidia had been co-operative with any efforts to get to the bottom of whether the company or Huang potentially knew about any chips being diverted to China, Blanche said: "I have no reason to stand up here and say Nvidia is anything but a good corporate citizen.
"Obviously, if Nvidia was the target or was subject to some criminal investigation or they were obstructing or thwarting our investigation, then that wouldn't be the message that the president is saying to the American people.
"It shouldn't be what my message would be either."
While Nvidia's stock market value surged on the announcement of Huang's reappointment, some of the gains were reversed in volatile Tuesday trading.
The company's share price closed down nearly 6% - still well above where it ended last week. On Monday, Nvidia stock rocketed more than 31% following news of Huang's return.
The company's board reinstated Huang on Monday in a shock U-turn. Harvey Jones, chairman of Nvidia's board, said Huang's return was in the "best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers".
The board said it had received input from senior levels of the US government and was confident that Huang's reinstatement posed no national security risk.
On Monday, Trump said he spoke to the company's directors and convinced them to bring back Huang .
Huang's reinstatement provoked bipartisan anger.
Republican congressman Don Bacon said Nvidia should have "ignored the Administration's inexplicable desire to save Huang".
Republican Senator Pete Ricketts said Huang's behaviour "doesn't absolve Nvidia of answering for national security concerns and unaccounted-for chips".
Democratic congressman Robert Garcia, the incoming chairman of the House oversight committee, said Trump's "direct involvement" with Nvidia's decision "raises serious national security and corruption questions".
Democratic Senator Ruben Gallego said Congress needed to "investigate what stock positions took place before the announcement".

articles.title_orig: Anthropic Shares Plunge 8% Below IPO Price in Fourth Trading Day
articles.title_zh: Anthropic Shares Plunge 8% Below IPO Price in Fourth Trading Day
articles.content_orig:
Anthropic shares are back trading below the IPO price after a 13% sell-off Tuesday and a 1.5% drop Monday, despite a broad rally in most big tech artificial intelligence names. Trading under $76 on Tuesday, the stock's now 8.5% below its initial public offering level and 34% beneath its intraday high of $115.
It took just four days for ANT to fall under its offering price, compared with 21 trading days for SpaceX , which rallied out of the gate.
Options volume on the stock is picking up as the shares drop and implied volatility jumps to 96, according to ThinkOrSwim data. Almost 500,000 options traded by noon ET on Tuesday for a total premium of about $250 million, the sixth-most active single-stock options in the market, SpotGamma data shows.
Almost 300,000 puts traded versus about 200,000 calls, but the sentiment implied by the trades was not overtly bearish, and judging by the biggest single trades of the day, traders are divided on what happens next.
The biggest single option trade of the day was a $7.5 million purchase of almost 11,000 75-strike puts expiring in mid-December. The trader paid above the ask, suggesting an eagerness to get the trade done at a cost of $6.85, according to SpotGamma. With Anthropic trading at $77, the position needs Anthropic to drop 11% by expiry to pay off.
"Anthropic remains bumpy as investors add risk to other names," said noted tech analyst Dan Ives.
Only one obvious call purchase appeared among the top 10 trades: a 3,000-lot purchase of 85-strike calls expiring Jan. 15 that cost $7.10 each, for a total of $2.2 million. That trade needs Anthropic to rally 19% within the next two months to break even.
Arguably the most interesting action was a string of almost a dozen put sales, ranging from $400,000 to $1.6 million each, all within moments of each other, selling the 120-strike puts expiring Dec. 18. The puts bring in $40 each, meaning the breakeven for the trade is at $80. Selling in-the-money puts in high-volatility stocks is often a way for traders to get long stock without the capital requirements of buying the underlying equity.

articles.title_orig: Tesla, SpaceX Reportedly Pick Board Members To Negotiate Elon Musk's Mega Merger
articles.title_zh: Tesla, SpaceX Reportedly Pick Board Members To Negotiate Elon Musk's Mega Merger
articles.content_orig:
Two communities in Texas and Arizona are holding votes next month to determine the future of SpaceX data center plans in their areas.
On December 9, the Cochise County Planning and Zoning Commission in Arizona and the Starbase City Commission are both scheduled to vote on proposals related to the data center project. The two votes center around a special land use authorization and a tax incentive package for the data centers.
SpaceX plans to spend more than $74 billion on two AI supercomputing campuses, making them two of the largest data center projects in the country.
"These investments will expand local tax bases, generate substantial new revenue for schools and public services, and create economic opportunities that extend far beyond the facilities themselves," SpaceX said on its website.
In Texas, SpaceX plans to invest $24 billion in a 444-acre plot in Brownsville, near its own Starbase rocket site in the Rio Grande Valley. SpaceX said the project has already created more than 3,000 construction jobs, with more than 500 permanent jobs coming once its operations begin. It also pledged $200 million to expand Brownsville's water and wastewater infrastructure.
The company added that the facility is designed to "stand on its own" by generating its own electricity rather than pulling from the public power grid.
The City Commission of the City of Starbase will convene on December 9 to consider approval of a 10-year, 100 percent property tax abatement. Starbase City officials declined to comment to Newsweek .
Last week, the Cameron County commission voted against a tax break for the SpaceX data center. The company sought a tax break in Starbase, where two of the three City Commission members are current SpaceX employees.
"As Texas communities consider major supercomputing investments, careful long-term tax planning is essential," SpaceX said. "The proposed abatement was designed to address this challenge: provide the County with substantial, predictable new revenue through payments in lieu of taxes (PILOTs), incentivize continued investment and meet the County’s economic development goals."
The project was granted an air pollution permit by the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ) after outgoing Republican Governor Greg Abbott directed the regulatory agency to pause all data center permits until it completes its impact evaluations.
Newly-elected Governor Gina Hinojosa, a Democrat, made halting data center construction a pillar of her campaign to ensure lawmakers can provide adequate protections for Texans.
SpaceX also plans to build a $50 billion, 747-acre data center in Cochise County, Arizona, about 80 miles east of Tucson.
According to the proposal, SpaceX said the plan would reduce electricity bills by up to 20 percent and create 1,000 permanent jobs. This facility would also use a dry cooling system and would not pump groundwater for industrial use, but local residents worry about the already strained aquifer.
The Cochise County Planning and Zoning board will vote on the s pecial use authorization f or Tombstone Resource LCC, the company building the SpaceX data center. This vote will determine if the project is allowed to proceed under current zoning rules.
On November 19, Attorney General Kris Mayes asked the county to postpone the December 9 vote until state and federal agencies could provide a full review of the project.
"The people of Cochise County deserve answers before county officials approve a project of this magnitude," Mayes said in a statement. "The company’s proposal raises serious unanswered questions about energy reliability, water use, emergency response capabilities, traffic impacts and effects on surrounding communities. Those issues must be fully examined by the appropriate state and federal agencies before any local approval moves forward."
In her letter, Mayes said the project could consume up to six gigawatts of electricity, which is nearly 20 percent of the state's current power-generating capacity, and could strain the local groundwater supplies. She also highlighted concerns about traffic, strains on local emergency service resources and the impact on local wildlife.
She said the company's proposal leaves a lot about the project uncertain, saying that "the sheer scale of its power demand and physical size presents exorbitant risks," and reminded the commission of its duty to ensure the development is feasible before construction is approved.
Mayes will host a town hall scheduled for Thursday, December 3, for residents to voice concerns.
Newsweek reached out to Cochise County officials, Attorney General Mayes and SpaceX for comment.

articles.title_orig: Armed men hold hostages at supermarket in top Colombian tourist destination
articles.title_zh: Armed men hold hostages at supermarket in top Colombian tourist destination
articles.content_orig:
A group of armed men with their faces covered seized a supermarket in the Colombian city of Cartagena on Tuesday and are holding an unknown number of hostages, Colombian police said.
President Abelardo de la Espriella said that the men were "common criminals" who fled into the supermarket after a failed attempt to hold up an armored truck.
The hostage situation broke out as Colombia is experiencing a wave of attacks by rebel groups on government targets, which has recently spread to urban areas.
Footage shared on social media showed dozens of people rushing out of an Exito supermarket in Cartagena's La Castellana neighborhood, while local media have broadcast images of snipers on nearby buildings in what appears to be a standoff between the armed men and police.
Cartagena is one of Colombia's main tourist destinations. The city of a million people is famous for its well-preserved 18th-century architecture and the thick stone walls built to defend it from pirate attacks.
Cartagena's airport temporarily suspended its operations on Tuesday following the incident. But it later said in a social media post that operations were slowly returning to normal.
